questions.stem: Typical elastic arteries:

options.label: A
options.text: Possess a thick tunica media

options.label: B
options.text: Possess a thick tunica media with many concentric, fenestrated, elastic laminae

options.label: C
options.text: Possess a thick tunica media with smooth muscle fibers

options.label: D
options.text: Possess series of valves throughout their length

options.label: E
options.text: Contract during diastole to help propel blood forward

notes.A: A large elastic artery such as the aorta has a thick media adapted to pulsatile pressure.
notes.B: Concentric sheets of fenestrated elastin stretch during systole and spring back during diastole.
notes.C: Smooth muscle cells between the elastic laminae help maintain the extracellular matrix of the media.
notes.D: Valves occur in many peripheral veins. Elastic arteries have no series of valves along their course.
notes.E: Diastolic forward flow is driven by release of stored elastic energy. It does not require active arterial contraction.

questions.why: Elastic laminae in the thick arterial media stretch during ventricular ejection. The wall then recoils passively during diastole, maintaining forward blood flow as ventricular ejection pauses.

questions.stem: Functions of the lymphatic system include:

options.label: A
options.text: Body immunity and filtration of lymph

options.label: B
options.text: Absorption of fats and collection of cellular debris

options.label: C
options.text: Drainage of tissue fluid

options.label: D
options.text: Production of lymphocytes

notes.A: Lymph nodes trap material arriving from tissues and bring lymph-borne antigens into contact with lymphocytes.
notes.B: Intestinal lacteals take up chylomicrons, and lymphatic drainage carries cellular debris away from tissues.
notes.C: Blind-ended lymphatic capillaries collect excess interstitial fluid for return to the venous circulation.
notes.D: Lymphocytes develop in primary lymphoid organs and proliferate after activation in secondary lymphoid organs.

questions.why: Lymphatics return excess interstitial fluid and carry dietary lipids from the gut. Lymphoid tissues filter lymph, expose antigens to immune cells, and support lymphocyte development or expansion.

questions.stem: Lymph nodes:

options.label: A
options.text: Filter lymph and blood and have a single efferent lymphatic vessel that leaves via the hilum

options.label: B
options.text: Have afferent lymphatic vessels that enter the convex edge of the node and empty into the marginal sinus

options.label: C
options.text: Have medullary regions that are formed by irregular strands and cords of lymphoid tissue that alternate with lymph sinuses

notes.A: Nodes filter lymph, while the spleen filters blood. One or more efferent lymphatics leave a node at its hilum.
notes.B: Afferent lymphatics pierce the convex capsule and empty into the subcapsular sinus, also called the marginal sinus.
notes.C: Medullary cords contain lymphoid cells and plasma cells. They alternate with sinuses that carry lymph towards the hilum.

questions.why: Afferent lymphatics deliver lymph to the subcapsular sinus at the convex surface. Lymph then passes through cortical and medullary sinuses and exits at the hilum.

questions.stem: The thymic medulla contains:

options.label: A
options.text: Hassall’s corpuscles and lymphoid nodules with germinal centres

options.label: B
options.text: Central arteries and marginal zones

options.label: C
options.text: Large venous sinusoids and Billroth’s cords

options.label: D
options.text: A whirl-like arrangement of epithelial reticular cells

options.label: E
options.text: Diffuse lymphoid tissue

notes.A: Hassall’s corpuscles are medullary, but the normal thymus lacks the follicles and germinal centres seen in secondary lymphoid organs.
notes.B: A central arteriole within white pulp and a marginal zone are characteristic features of the spleen.
notes.C: Venous sinusoids and the cords of Billroth belong to the splenic red pulp.
notes.D: Concentric whorls of epithelial reticular cells form Hassall’s corpuscles within the thymic medulla.
notes.E: Maturing T cells are dispersed among epithelial reticular cells, giving the medulla a paler appearance than the cortex.

questions.why: The thymic medulla has relatively sparse thymocytes among epithelial reticular cells. Concentric layers of those epithelial cells form Hassall’s corpuscles, a distinctive feature of the medulla.

questions.stem: The thymus:

options.label: A
options.text: Lacks both afferent lymphatic vessels and lymphoid nodules

options.label: B
options.text: Has a cortex and a medulla based largely on different concentrations of lymphocytes

options.label: C
options.text: Has a capsule from which trabeculae extend into the interior of the organ to form partial lobules

options.label: D
options.text: Produces T- lymphocytes and involutes rapidly after puberty

options.label: E
options.text: Has a perivascular connective tissue sheath in the cortex that is ensheathed by the epithelial reticular cells

notes.A: Thymocyte precursors arrive through blood vessels. The thymic parenchyma lacks afferent lymphatics and normal lymphoid follicles.
notes.B: Closely packed immature thymocytes stain the cortex dark. The medulla has fewer lymphocytes and stains more lightly.
notes.C: Septa from the capsule divide the cortex into partial lobules while leaving the medulla continuous.
notes.D: Bone marrow precursors mature into T cells in the thymus. After puberty its lymphoid tissue is progressively replaced by fat.
notes.E: Cortical epithelial reticular cells enclose perivascular connective tissue and contribute to the blood–thymus barrier.

questions.why: The thymus has dark, thymocyte-rich cortices around paler medullary regions that are continuous between lobules. It supports T-cell maturation, and its functional parenchyma declines after puberty.

questions.stem: The spleen:

options.label: A
options.text: White pulp contains nodular regions and non-nodular regions that are comparable to the cortex of a lymph node

options.label: B
options.text: Sinuses are defined, endothelium-lined vascular channels that branch and anastomose irregularly

options.label: C
options.text: The red pulp is formed by two vascular compartments, sinuses and Billroth’s cords

options.label: D
options.text: The red pulp resembles the lymphatic sinuses and medullary cords in the medulla of the lymph node

options.label: E
options.text: Red pulp Cords are made up of a three-dimensional meshwork of reticular cells and reticular fibres with macrophages

notes.A: White pulp has B-cell follicles like nodal follicles and periarteriolar T-cell sheaths functionally comparable to the nodal paracortex.
notes.B: Branched venous sinuses have a lining of elongated endothelial cells separated by narrow slits.
notes.C: Red pulp contains venous sinuses and the intervening cords of Billroth. In the open circulation, blood passes through the cords before entering the sinuses.
notes.D: Both red pulp and nodal medulla have cords between sinuses. Splenic sinuses carry blood, and nodal sinuses carry lymph.
notes.E: Splenic cords contain a mesh of reticular cells and fibres with macrophages that remove ageing erythrocytes.

questions.why: Splenic white pulp mounts responses to blood-borne antigens. Blood passes through the red pulp, where macrophages screen cells and deformable erythrocytes can enter venous sinuses.

questions.stem: All of the following about the spleen are true EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: Is the site of the largest accumulation of lymphoid tissue in the human body

options.label: B
options.text: Is the site of destruction of red blood cells

options.label: C
options.text: Is for the production of lymphocytes and immune responses

options.label: D
options.text: Contains plasma cells, macrophages and reticular fibers

options.label: E
options.text: Contains venous sinusoids which act as the main filters of foreign particles

questions.why: Phagocytes in the marginal zone and red pulp remove foreign material from blood. The narrow slits of the venous sinuses chiefly select for red cells able to deform.

notes.A: The spleen is the largest single lymphoid organ. Its white pulp forms lymphoid tissue around central arterioles.
notes.B: Ageing and damaged erythrocytes can be retained in the red pulp and removed by macrophages.
notes.C: White pulp lymphocytes proliferate after activation and mount adaptive responses to antigens arriving in blood.
notes.D: Reticular fibres support the splenic cords, where macrophages and antibody-secreting plasma cells can be found.

questions.stem: Functions performed by EVERY lymphoid organ:

options.label: A
options.text: Filtration of lymph

options.label: B
options.text: Production of lymphocytes

options.label: C
options.text: Destruction of blood cells

options.label: D
options.text: Filtration of blood

options.label: E
options.text: Production of reticular fibers

notes.A: Lymph nodes have afferent vessels that carry lymph into them. The spleen and thymus lack this incoming route.
notes.B: Developing lymphocytes proliferate in primary organs. In secondary organs, mature lymphocytes proliferate in response to antigen.
notes.C: Splenic red pulp macrophages remove ageing erythrocytes. Other lymphoid organs do not share this role as a defining function.
notes.D: The spleen screens blood directly, whereas lymph nodes principally sample lymph arriving from peripheral tissues.
notes.E: The thymic parenchyma uses an epithelial reticular scaffold. Lymph nodes and spleen have reticular fibre frameworks.

questions.why: Lymphocyte numbers increase during development in primary lymphoid organs and during immune responses in secondary organs. Filtration and stromal structure vary with the organ’s role.

questions.stem: The jejunum differs from the duodenum mainly by the ABSENCE of:

options.label: A
options.text: Relatively large submucosal collections of lymphoid tissue in its submucosa known as Peyer’s patches

options.label: B
options.text: Simple, test-tube shaped invaginations of the mucosa known as crypts of Lieberkuhn

options.label: C
options.text: Prominent plicae circulares

options.label: D
options.text: Brunner’s glands

options.label: E
options.text: Chief cells

questions.why: Duodenal submucosa contains Brunner’s glands, which release alkaline mucus to protect the mucosa from incoming gastric acid. Jejunal sections lack these submucosal glands.

notes.A: Large aggregated Peyer’s patches are characteristic of the ileum, so their absence cannot distinguish jejunum from duodenum.
notes.B: Intestinal crypts are present in the mucosa of both the duodenum and jejunum and renew the epithelium in each.
notes.C: The jejunum has particularly prominent circular folds, which increase the area of mucosa available for absorption.
notes.E: Chief cells produce pepsinogen in gastric glands and are absent from both these small intestinal segments.

questions.stem: Swell bodies of the nasal conchae perform all of the following EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: Sensory perception

options.label: B
options.text: Adjustment of the temperature of inspired air

options.label: C
options.text: Regulation of blood flow to the overlying epithelium

options.label: D
options.text: Increasing contact between inspired air and the nasal mucosa

options.label: E
options.text: Increasing pressure in the nasal cavity

questions.why: Swell bodies warm air and adjust flow; they have no sensory role.

notes.B: A function.
notes.C: A function.
notes.D: A function.
notes.E: A function.

questions.stem: The nasal cavity has:

options.label: A
options.text: 3 bony shelf-like projections known as conchae/turbinates

options.label: B
options.text: An inferior concha covered by a specialized olfactory epithelium

options.label: C
options.text: Superior and middle conchae covered by respiratory epithelium

options.label: D
options.text: Turbinates which increase the surface area and cause turbulence in airflow to allow more efficient conditioning of inspired air

options.label: E
options.text: Narrow, ribbon-like passages created by the conchae resulting in increased contact between the Streams of air and the mucous layer

notes.A: Each lateral nasal wall usually has superior, middle and inferior conchae along its height.
notes.B: The inferior concha is covered mainly by respiratory epithelium and helps warm and humidify inspired air.
notes.C: Much of the conchal surface has respiratory lining, but olfactory epithelium occupies part of the superior conchal region.
notes.D: The shelves increase nasal surface area and redirect airflow, bringing it close to the vascular, mucus-lined mucosa.
notes.E: Narrow meatuses guide streams of air close to the mucus layer, where particles can be trapped.

questions.why: Conchae increase the mucosal surface in contact with inspired air and redirect it through narrow meatuses. Respiratory mucosa conditions the air, and olfactory mucosa occupies more superior patches.

questions.stem: Paranasal sinuses:

options.label: A
options.text: Are air-filled spaces in the bones of the walls of the nasal cavity

options.label: B
options.text: Are located in the ethmoid, sphenoid, frontal, maxillary, palatine and lacrimal bones

options.label: C
options.text: Are lined with a thinner respiratory epithelium that contains goblet cells

options.label: D
options.text: Communicate with the nasal cavities via narrow openings onto the respiratory mucosa

notes.A: The spaces lie in bones surrounding the nasal cavity and are normally filled with air.
notes.B: The frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid and maxillary bones contain the named sinuses. The palatine and lacrimal bones do not.
notes.C: Sinus lining is generally thinner than nasal respiratory mucosa and has relatively few mucus-secreting goblet cells.
notes.D: Each sinus communicates with the nasal cavity through an ostium that permits ventilation and mucus drainage.

questions.why: The paranasal sinuses are air spaces within the frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid and maxillary bones. Their thin respiratory lining clears mucus through small openings into the nasal cavity.

questions.stem: The pharynx:

options.label: A
options.text: Is a musculofibrous half-cylinder that links the oral and nasal cavities to the larynx and oesophagus

options.label: B
options.text: Serves as a passageway for air and food and provides a resonating chamber for speech

options.label: C
options.text: Diffuse lymphatic tissue and lymphatic nodules are found in its wall

options.label: D
options.text: Is lined by pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium with goblets and stratified squamous non- keratinized epithelium

options.label: E
options.text: Is connected to the middle ear by the auditory (Eustachian) tubes

notes.A: Its partially open anterior wall communicates with the nasal cavity, oral cavity and larynx. Inferiorly it continues into the oesophagus.
notes.B: The pharynx conducts air and food and modifies voice resonance through its shape and size.
notes.C: Pharyngeal lymphoid tissue includes diffuse lymphocytes and organised follicles, particularly in the tonsils.
notes.D: Ciliated respiratory epithelium covers much of the nasopharynx. Non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium protects surfaces exposed to food.
notes.E: Each auditory tube connects the lateral nasopharynx to the middle ear and allows pressure equalisation across the tympanic membrane.

questions.why: The pharynx is a fibromuscular passage shared by air and food. Its lining changes from respiratory epithelium in much of the nasopharynx to abrasion-resistant squamous epithelium lower down.

questions.stem: The larynx:

options.label: A
options.text: Is an air passage, an organ of phonation and a sphincteric mechanism that closes the lower respiratory tract

options.label: B
options.text: Is part of the respiratory portion of the respiratory system

options.label: C
options.text: Has three unpaired hyaline cartilages; cricoid, thyroid and epiglottis

options.label: D
options.text: Has three pairs of elastic cartilages; arytenoids, corniculates and cuneiform

options.label: E
options.text: Has a fibroelastic membrane and numerous intrinsic skeletal muscles

notes.A: The larynx provides a conducting airway and produces sound. Closure at several levels helps protect the trachea during swallowing.
notes.B: The larynx is in the conducting portion. Gas exchange begins distally in respiratory bronchioles with alveoli in their walls.
notes.C: The thyroid and cricoid are hyaline cartilage. The leaf-shaped epiglottis is supported by elastic cartilage.
notes.D: Most arytenoid cartilage is hyaline. The corniculates, cuneiforms and portions of the arytenoids contain elastic cartilage.
notes.E: Fibroelastic membranes support the laryngeal folds, and intrinsic muscles change vocal fold position or tension.

questions.why: The larynx conducts air, produces voice and closes to protect the lower airway. Its cartilaginous framework and fibroelastic membranes are moved by intrinsic skeletal muscles.

questions.stem: The epiglottis:

options.label: A
options.text: Is a leaf-shaped cartilage attached by its stem to the posterior aspect of the thyroid cartilage at the thyroid angle

options.label: B
options.text: Has below it, a pair of mucosal folds that lack muscle and are covered by pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium with goblets

options.label: C
options.text: Contains mixed mucous and serous glands and hyaline cartilage

notes.A: Its stalk attaches to the back of the thyroid angle.
notes.B: The vestibular (false) folds below it are mostly glands and loose connective tissue with little or no muscle, unlike the vocal folds, and are covered by respiratory epithelium.
notes.C: Its glands are mixed, but its cartilage is elastic, not hyaline.

questions.why: The epiglottis is a leaf of elastic cartilage attached to the thyroid angle; below it lie the vestibular (false) folds, which are mainly glands and connective tissue rather than muscle.

questions.stem: Bronchi:

options.label: A
options.text: The wall of the bronchi is structurally similar to the mucosa of the trachea except for the organization of cartilage and smooth muscle,

options.label: B
options.text: Are air passages for air conduction, filtration and warming

options.label: C
options.text: Have a band of muscle reinforced with elastic fibres at the junction of the submucosa and lamina propria

notes.A: Intrapulmonary bronchi retain a respiratory lining but have cartilage plates and a circumferential muscle layer rather than the tracheal arrangement.
notes.B: Bronchi conduct air towards the gas-exchange regions. Their mucociliary surface clears particles and their mucosa helps warm the air.
notes.C: Smooth muscle with elastic fibres lies around the lamina propria, superficial to the submucosa and its glands.

questions.why: Intrapulmonary bronchi maintain respiratory epithelium and submucosal glands. Irregular cartilage plates replace the tracheal rings, and a smooth muscle layer deep to the mucosa regulates airway calibre.

questions.stem: Bronchioles:

options.label: A
options.text: Are intralobular airways with diameters of 1 mm or less without cartilages and glands

options.label: B
options.text: Have pseudostratified columnar ciliated with goblet cells or simple columnar ciliated with goblet cells and simple cuboidal ciliated epithelium with Clara cells

options.label: C
options.text: Have a relatively thick layer of smooth muscle

options.label: D
options.text: Have Clara cells that secrete a surface-active agent, a lipoprotein to prevent luminal adhesion

options.label: E
options.text: Has a muscularis that is under the control of the vagus nerve and the sympathetic nervous system

notes.A: Bronchioles are 1 mm or less and have no cartilage or glands.
notes.B: The epithelium changes from ciliated columnar with goblet cells to cuboidal with Clara (club) cells.
notes.C: Their smooth muscle layer is relatively thick for their size.
notes.D: Clara (club) cells secrete a surfactant-like lipoprotein that stops the walls sticking.
notes.E: The vagus constricts and sympathetic nerves dilate them.

questions.why: Bronchioles lack cartilage and glands, so their relatively thick, autonomically controlled smooth muscle sets airway calibre; club (Clara) cells replace goblet cells distally.

questions.stem: Respiratory bronchioles:

options.label: A
options.text: Have walls that are interrupted by numerous alveoli for gas exchange

options.label: B
options.text: Have simple cuboidal ciliated epithelial cells with Clara cells and simple squamous epithelium

options.label: C
options.text: Have smooth muscle and elastic connective tissue

options.label: D
options.text: Are continuous with terminal bronchioles and alveolar ducts

options.label: E
options.text: Have Type I alveolar cells

notes.A: Alveolar openings interrupt the bronchiolar wall, providing the first sites for gas exchange along the airway.
notes.B: Cuboidal cells and club cells line the airway segments, with ciliated cells most evident proximally. Alveoli have thin squamous lining cells.
notes.C: Smooth muscle and elastic fibres persist in the wall segments between adjacent alveolar openings.
notes.D: Respiratory bronchioles follow terminal bronchioles and lead into alveolar ducts with more extensive alveolar openings.
notes.E: Thin type I pneumocytes line most of the surface of each alveolar outpocketing and shorten the diffusion distance.

questions.why: Respiratory bronchioles are the first airways with alveoli opening out of their walls. The bronchiolar segments still have cuboidal epithelium and smooth muscle, while the alveoli permit gas exchange.

questions.stem: Alveoli:

options.label: A
options.text: Have a lining of Type I and II Alveolar Cells and Occasional Brush Cells

options.label: B
options.text: Form the mass of the parenchyma of the lung, giving the appearance of fine lace or a sponge

options.label: C
options.text: Are the terminal air spaces of the respiratory system and are the actual sites of gas exchange Between the air and the blood

options.label: D
options.text: Have very thin squamous cells covering about 95% of the alveolar surface

options.label: E
options.text: Have cuboidal secretory cells covering about 5% of the surface, mainly at septal junctions

notes.A: They are lined by type I and II cells with occasional brush cells.
notes.B: They form most of the lung parenchyma, giving its spongy look.
notes.C: They are the terminal air spaces where gas exchange takes place.
notes.D: Type I cells cover about 95% of the surface.
notes.E: Type II cells cover about 5%, mainly at septal junctions.

questions.why: Alveoli are the gas-exchange spaces: thin type I cells cover about 95% of the surface and cuboidal type II cells, which make surfactant, the rest.

questions.stem: Pulmonary surfactant:

options.label: A
options.text: Forms a monomolecular layer over the alveolar epithelium

options.label: B
options.text: Reduces the surface tension at the air-epithelium interface

options.label: C
options.text: The alveoli would collapse on exhalation without adequate secretions of surfactant

options.label: D
options.text: Inadequate secretions of surfactant causes respiratory distress syndrome

options.label: E
options.text: Is secreted by the type II pneumocyte cuboidal secretory cells

notes.A: Surfactant spreads as a thin surface film at the air-facing boundary of the alveolar lining fluid.
notes.B: Surface-active phospholipids reduce cohesive forces at the air–liquid interface and lower alveolar surface tension.
notes.C: Without adequate surfactant, surface tension increases the tendency of small alveoli to collapse during expiration.
notes.D: Insufficient surfactant in premature infants contributes to low lung compliance and neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.
notes.E: Cuboidal type II pneumocytes store surfactant in lamellar bodies and release it onto the alveolar surface.

questions.why: Type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant at the alveolar air–liquid interface. It lowers surface tension as alveoli get smaller in expiration, improving compliance and resisting collapse.

questions.stem: The alveolar septum:

options.label: A
options.text: Consists of the Alveolar epithelial cells, Basal lamina of the alveolar epithelium, Basal lamina of the capillary endothelium, Endothelial cells of the rich capillary network

options.label: B
options.text: Consists of connective tissue elements, including fibroblasts, macrophages, collagen fibers, and elastic fibers

options.label: C
options.text: Has a thin portion consisting of a monomolecular layer of surfactant, a type I epithelial cell, a capillary endothelial cell and the fused basal lamina

options.label: D
options.text: Has a thick portion consisting of connective tissue cells and fibers between the two basal laminae

options.label: E
options.text: Gas exchange occurs across the thin portion of the barrier whereas the thick portion is a site for accumulation of tissue fluid

notes.A: The septum includes alveolar epithelium and capillary endothelium with their basal laminae. These laminae are fused at the thinnest sites.
notes.B: Fibroblasts, macrophages, collagen and elastic fibres are found in the interstitial part of the septum.
notes.C: The thin route crosses lining fluid and surfactant, a type I pneumocyte, the fused basal laminae and capillary endothelium.
notes.D: The thicker regions have connective tissue and cells between the separate epithelial and endothelial basal laminae.
notes.E: The thin side has the shortest diffusion path. Interstitial fluid can collect in the thicker connective tissue compartment.

questions.why: The thinnest alveolar septum has fused epithelial and endothelial basal laminae that minimise the gas diffusion distance. Thicker regions contain interstitial connective tissue and can accommodate more tissue fluid.

questions.stem: Alveolar macrophages:

options.label: A
options.text: Remove inhaled particulate matter from the air spaces and red blood cells from the septum

options.label: B
options.text: Function both in the connective tissue of the septum and in the air space of the alveolus

options.label: C
options.text: May remain in the septal connective tissue and may stay for much of an individual’s life

options.label: D
options.text: That are filled with carbon particles are present in lungs of a smoker at autopsy

options.label: E
options.text: Phagocytose infectious organisms such as tubercle bacilli

notes.A: These phagocytes clear particulates from air spaces and can remove extravasated erythrocytes from the septum.
notes.B: Macrophages occur both within the alveolar lumen and in connective tissue of the alveolar septum.
notes.C: Some pigment-bearing macrophages remain in the septal interstitium for years, especially if the particles are indigestible.
notes.D: Inhaled carbon can remain visible as dark pigment inside macrophages, including in tissue from smokers.
notes.E: Alveolar macrophages can engulf inhaled mycobacteria. Phagocytosis alone does not guarantee that the organisms are killed.

questions.why: Alveolar macrophages patrol the air spaces and septal connective tissue. They engulf inhaled particles and microbes and remove erythrocytes that leak into alveolar tissue or air spaces.

questions.stem: The olfactory segment of the nasal cavity has:

options.label: A
options.text: A slight yellowish-brown colour due to the presence of pigment in the olfactory epithelium and olfactory glands

options.label: B
options.text: A pseudostratified columnar epithelium with Olfactory cells, sustentacular cells and goblet cells

options.label: C
options.text: Tubuloalveolar glands that produce a watery serous secretion for washing and trapping of odorant substances and renewal of the olfactory sensation

options.label: D
options.text: A lamina propria with olfactory nerves in combination with the olfactory glands

options.label: E
options.text: Bipolar neurons that are replaced during postnatal life

notes.A: Pigment in the olfactory mucosa gives the region its characteristic yellowish to yellow-brown appearance.
notes.B: The pseudostratified olfactory lining contains receptor neurons, sustentacular cells and basal cells. Goblet cells characterise adjacent respiratory epithelium.
notes.C: Serous secretion from Bowman’s glands dissolves odorants and helps wash previously bound stimuli away.
notes.D: Bundles of olfactory receptor axons run through the lamina propria beside the glands and towards the cribriform plate.
notes.E: Basal progenitor cells can differentiate into new bipolar olfactory receptor neurons after birth.

questions.why: Olfactory mucosa contains receptor neurons with supporting and basal cells. Serous secretion from Bowman’s glands dissolves odorants and clears them from the sensory surface.

questions.stem: The tongue:

options.label: A
options.text: The mucosa of the ventral surface of the tongue is modified to form papillae

options.label: B
options.text: Is a mass of skeletal muscle that runs in different planes

options.label: C
options.text: Has whitish areas which are due to the presence of numerous highly keratinised filiform papillae and reddish rounded areas of fungiform papillae among the filiform papillae

options.label: D
options.text: Has glands that are interspersed among the skeletal muscle fibres

options.label: E
options.text: Has taste receptors in all the papillae

notes.A: Lingual papillae are on the dorsum. The ventral surface has thin, smooth lining mucosa.
notes.B: Muscle bundles cross in different planes, allowing the tongue to change shape as well as position.
notes.C: Keratin makes filiform tips appear whitish. Vessels show through the thinner epithelium of fungiform papillae, giving a reddish appearance.
notes.D: Minor salivary glands lie among muscle bundles. Their ducts release secretions onto the tongue surface.
notes.E: Filiform papillae provide friction for handling food and lack the taste buds found in the other papillary types.

questions.why: Interlacing skeletal muscle allows the tongue to change shape during speech and swallowing. Its dorsal papillae have different functions, and the ventral mucosa is smooth.

questions.stem: The stomach has:

options.label: A
options.text: Peptic cells which secrete pepsin and intrinsic factor

options.label: B
options.text: A mucus-secreting epithelium which helps to protect the gastric mucosa from autodigestion and its own highly acidic secretion

options.label: C
options.text: Gastric pits that serve as short ducts for conveying gastric secretions from the mucosal glands to the lumen of the stomach

options.label: D
options.text: Parietal cells secrete HCL, gastrin and Pepsin

options.label: E
options.text: Rugae that are composed of the mucosa and the underlying submucosa

notes.A: Chief cells release inactive pepsinogen. Acid activates it in the lumen, and intrinsic factor is secreted by parietal cells.
notes.B: Surface mucous cells produce mucus and bicarbonate, which help protect the epithelium from acid and pepsin.
notes.C: A gastric pit is a surface invagination into which several mucosal glands can empty.
notes.D: Parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor. G cells release gastrin and chief cells release pepsinogen.
notes.E: Rugae consist of mucosa and submucosa. They flatten when the stomach distends after a meal.

questions.why: Gastric chief cells release pepsinogen, while parietal cells provide acid and intrinsic factor. Gastric pits collect gland secretions, and a bicarbonate-rich mucus barrier protects the mucosal surface.

questions.stem: A loop of small intestine is identified as jejunum rather than ileum because the:

options.label: A
options.text: Jejunum has a greater diameter and a thicker wall due to the plicae circulares

options.label: B
options.text: Jejunal arterial arcades are simple or double with long vasa recti while the ileal arcades are Multiple with short vasa recti

options.label: C
options.text: Ileum has shorter club-shaped villi

options.label: D
options.text: Ileum contains more goblet cells and ileal mesentery contains more fat making it opaque

options.label: E
options.text: Ileum has more lymphoid nodules

notes.A: The jejunum typically has a wider lumen and thicker wall with taller, more closely spaced circular folds.
notes.B: The proximal jejunum has fewer tiers of arcades and longer vasa recta. Ileal arcades have more tiers and shorter straight vessels.
notes.C: Ileal villi are generally shorter and often blunter than those of the jejunum.
notes.D: Goblet cell density generally increases distally. Ileal mesenteric fat often extends to the bowel margin and obscures the vessels.
notes.E: Aggregated lymphoid nodules called Peyer’s patches are particularly prominent in the distal ileum.

questions.why: The jejunum typically has taller circular folds and longer vasa recta. Greater mesenteric fat, more arterial arcades and aggregated lymphoid nodules favour ileum, particularly distally.

questions.stem: Following a barium meal in a normal person, the outline of the barium shadow in the first part of the duodenum was smooth. In the remaining parts of the duodenum. The barium was broken up, giving a floccular appearance. These differences in appearance are due to the:

options.label: A
options.text: Absence of plicae circulares in the first part of the duodenum and numerous plicae circulares in the remaining parts of the duodenum

options.label: B
options.text: Absence of lymphoid nodules in the first part of the duodenum and numerous lymphoid nodules in the remaining parts of the duodenum

options.label: C
options.text: Presence of plicae circulares in the first part of the duodenum and absence of plicae circulares in the remaining parts of the duodenum

options.label: D
options.text: Absence of villi in the first part of the duodenum and numerous villi in the remaining parts of the duodenum

options.label: E
options.text: Absence of muscle in the first part of the duodenum and a prominent muscle layer in the remaining parts of the duodenum

questions.why: The proximal duodenal bulb usually has a smooth outline because prominent circular folds are absent there. Distally, barium outlines folds of mucosa and submucosa.

notes.B: Lymphoid nodules are immune tissue and do not produce the repeated transverse contrast pattern of circular folds.
notes.C: This reverses the distribution. The proximal bulb is smooth and the circular folds become prominent farther along the duodenum.
notes.D: Villi are microscopic mucosal projections throughout the duodenum, including the bulb. Larger circular folds account for this contrast pattern.
notes.E: A muscularis externa is present throughout the duodenum. The contrast outlines folds projecting from the inner mucosa and submucosa.

questions.stem: The liver:

options.label: A
options.text: Hepatocytes are bathed by arterial and venous blood entering the liver via the hepatic artery and the portal vein respectively

options.label: B
options.text: Sinusoidal blood flows away from the central vein

options.label: C
options.text: Blood from the central vein ultimately drains into the inferior vena cava via the hepatic veins

options.label: D
options.text: Sinusoidal blood spaces are lined by discontinuous endothelial and Kupffer cells

options.label: E
options.text: Between two directly adjacent hepatocytes is a bile canaliculus

notes.A: Blood from both sources mixes in sinusoids. Fenestrated endothelium allows plasma solutes to reach hepatocytes through the space of Disse.
notes.B: Sinusoidal blood flows from the lobular periphery toward the central vein, which serves as the outlet.
notes.C: Central veins drain into larger collecting veins that join the hepatic veins, which empty into the inferior vena cava.
notes.D: Fenestrated sinusoidal endothelial cells form a discontinuous barrier, and Kupffer macrophages lie on its luminal side.
notes.E: Membranes of adjacent hepatocytes enclose the bile canaliculus. Tight junctions separate bile from the surrounding intercellular space.

questions.why: Portal venous and hepatic arterial blood mix in sinusoids and flow toward central veins. Bile travels in the opposite direction through canaliculi toward ducts in portal tracts.

questions.stem: Both a muscularis mucosae and a myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus are present in:

options.label: A
options.text: Uterus, uterine tube and vas deferens

options.label: B
options.text: Duodenum, ureter, tongue and epididymis

options.label: C
options.text: Ureter, oesophagus, ejacutory ducts, trachea

options.label: D
options.text: Jejunum, stomach, duodenum and oesophagus

options.label: E
options.text: Penis, gallbladder, urinary bladder and urethra

questions.why: The listed gut organs share a thin muscularis mucosae at the base of the mucosa and a myenteric plexus deeper between muscle layers of the muscularis externa.

notes.A: The uterus, uterine tube and vas deferens contain smooth muscle, but they do not have the gut’s muscularis mucosae and enteric plexus.
notes.B: The duodenum contains both structures. The ureter, tongue and epididymis lack this combination of gut wall features.
notes.C: The oesophagus has both. The ureter, ejaculatory ducts and trachea lack the characteristic myenteric plexus.
notes.E: The gallbladder lacks a distinct muscularis mucosae, and the urinary and genital structures lack the gut’s paired arrangement.

questions.stem: All of the following about the lips are true EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: The lips serve for suckling

options.label: B
options.text: The lips are associated with speech

options.label: C
options.text: The lips are responsible for keeping food in the mouth

options.label: D
options.text: The lips do not have muscular tissue

options.label: E
options.text: The lips are similar in structure to the cheeks

questions.why: Orbicularis oris provides a skeletal muscle core within the lips. Contraction changes lip shape and helps seal the oral opening during suckling, chewing and speech.

notes.A: During suckling the lips form a seal that helps maintain the negative pressure needed to draw milk into the mouth.
notes.B: The lips shape vowels and come together for bilabial speech sounds such as those beginning the words ‘pat’ and ‘bat’.
notes.C: Lip closure helps retain food in the oral cavity while the tongue and cheeks move it during chewing.
notes.E: Lips and cheeks both have external skin and internal oral mucosa with skeletal muscle between the surfaces.

questions.stem: The glomeruli are best described as being tufts of

options.label: A
options.text: Arteries

options.label: B
options.text: Veins

options.label: C
options.text: Venules

options.label: D
options.text: Capillaries

options.label: E
options.text: Arterioles

questions.why: A glomerulus is a tuft of fenestrated capillaries within Bowman’s capsule. Blood enters through an afferent arteriole, and an efferent arteriole carries it away after filtration.

notes.A: Renal arterial branches deliver blood upstream. The glomerular tuft itself has capillary walls adapted for filtration.
notes.B: Renal veins collect blood downstream of the kidney’s capillary beds. The tuft drains directly into an efferent arteriole.
notes.C: Venules receive blood after it has traversed downstream capillary beds. They do not make up the tuft inside Bowman’s capsule.
notes.E: Afferent and efferent arterioles lie at the vascular pole. The network between them is formed by capillaries.

questions.stem: Which artery lies on the boundary between the cortex and medulla of the kidney?

options.label: A
options.text: Lobar

options.label: B
options.text: Arcuate

options.label: C
options.text: Interlobar

options.label: D
options.text: Cortical radiate

options.label: E
options.text: Segmental

questions.why: Arcuate arteries curve along the bases of the renal pyramids at the corticomedullary junction. They give rise to cortical radiate arteries that ascend into the cortex.

notes.A: A lobar vessel supplies a renal lobe. The curved arteries at the pyramid bases are the arcuate branches.
notes.C: Interlobar arteries run in the renal columns between pyramids and give off arcuate arteries near the pyramid bases.
notes.D: Cortical radiate arteries branch from arcuate arteries and pass outward through the cortex, giving off afferent arterioles.
notes.E: Segmental arteries branch near the renal hilum to supply renal segments. They lie upstream of the arcuate arteries.

questions.stem: The glomerulus differs from other capillaries in the body in that it

options.label: A
options.text: Has a basement membrane

options.label: B
options.text: Is impermeable to most substances

options.label: C
options.text: Is drained by an efferent arteriole

options.label: D
options.text: Has a blood pressure much lower than other organ systems

options.label: E
options.text: Contains sinusoidal capillaries

questions.why: Glomerular capillaries lie between two arterioles. The efferent arteriole carries blood away and helps maintain the capillary hydrostatic pressure needed for filtration into Bowman’s space.

notes.A: Many capillaries have a basement membrane. In the glomerulus it is a specialised layer of the filtration barrier.
notes.B: The barrier allows water and small solutes through readily. It restricts cells and most large plasma proteins.
notes.D: Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure is greater than in many systemic capillary beds, favouring the formation of filtrate.
notes.E: Glomerular capillaries are fenestrated and have a continuous basement membrane. They are distinct from hepatic or splenic sinusoids.

questions.stem: The Filtration Barrier between the capillary lumen and urinary space consists of:

options.label: A
options.text: Capillary endothelium, podocyte layer and the Basement membrane separating the two

options.label: B
options.text: Capillary endothelium, macula densa, pedicel layer and the Basement membrane Be

options.label: C
options.text: Visceral endothelium, macula densa, pedicel layer and the Basement membrane s

options.label: D
options.text: Extraglomerular mesangium, macula densa, pedicel layer and the Basement membrane

options.label: E
options.text: Capillary endothelium, intraglomerular mesangium, visceral layer and the Basement Membrane

questions.why: Filtrate crosses fenestrated capillary endothelium, the shared glomerular basement membrane and the slit diaphragms between podocyte foot processes before entering Bowman’s urinary space.

notes.B: The macula densa is part of the distal tubule at the vascular pole and lies outside the filtration barrier.
notes.C: Podocytes form the visceral epithelium of Bowman’s capsule. The distal tubular macula densa is separate from the capillary filtration surface.
notes.D: Extraglomerular mesangial cells and the macula densa are at the vascular pole. They are components of the juxtaglomerular apparatus.
notes.E: Intraglomerular mesangial cells support the tuft between capillary loops. They are absent from the normal three-layer filtration pathway.

questions.stem: A patient continually passes large volumes of very dilute urine. This may be due to:

options.label: A
options.text: Excessive ADH secretion

options.label: B
options.text: Absence of ADH

options.label: C
options.text: Haematuria

options.label: D
options.text: Overproduction of aldosterone

options.label: E
options.text: Dilation of the afferent arterioles

questions.why: Vasopressin promotes aquaporin-2 insertion in collecting duct cells. When the hormone is absent, water reabsorption falls, producing persistent passage of large volumes of dilute urine.

notes.A: Excess vasopressin increases collecting duct water permeability and favours water retention with relatively concentrated urine.
notes.C: Haematuria is the presence of red cells in urine. It does not account for persistently high volumes of dilute urine.
notes.D: Aldosterone promotes distal sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion. It does not replace vasopressin’s control of water permeability.
notes.E: Afferent arteriolar dilation can raise glomerular filtration, but urine concentration still depends on collecting duct water handling.

questions.stem: The renal medulla:

options.label: A
options.text: Has 8-12 conical structures called medullary pyramids

options.label: B
options.text: Appears striated and consists of varying lengths of the straight portions of the proximal and distal tubules, the loops of Henle, collecting ducts and vasa recta

options.label: C
options.text: Appears striated and consists of varying lengths of the convoluted and straight portions of the proximal and distal tubules, the loops of Henle, collecting ducts and vasa recta

options.label: D
options.text: Appears granular and consists of the proximal and distal convoluted tubules, the loops of Henle, collecting ducts, medullary rays and coiled arteries

options.label: E
options.text: Contains podocytes, filtrate slits and macula densa

notes.A: The medulla is arranged as renal pyramids. Eight to twelve is a teaching estimate and the actual number varies.
notes.B: Straight tubular segments including the loops of Henle, collecting ducts and vasa recta run in parallel within the medulla.
notes.C: Convoluted proximal and distal tubules lie in the cortex. The medullary segments run mainly in straight, parallel courses.
notes.D: Medullary rays are bundles of straight tubules and ducts that project into the cortex, where the convoluted tubules also lie.
notes.E: Podocytes and filtration slits are in cortical renal corpuscles. The macula densa is adjacent to their vascular pole.

questions.why: Parallel tubular segments, collecting ducts and vasa recta give the renal medulla a striated appearance. Renal corpuscles and convoluted tubules lie in the cortex.

questions.stem: Parts of the nephron include:

options.label: A
options.text: The renal corpuscle and the proximal convoluted tubule

options.label: B
options.text: The renal corpuscle and the collecting tubule

options.label: C
options.text: The straight portion of the proximal tubule and thin limb of the loop of Henle

options.label: D
options.text: The collecting tubule and the distal convoluted tubule

options.label: E
options.text: Renal capsule, glomerulus, straight portion of the proximal tubule and thin limb of the loop of Henle

notes.B: The collecting tubule is not part.
notes.D: The collecting tubule is not part.

questions.why: The nephron: renal corpuscle, proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal tubule. Collecting tubules are separate.

questions.stem: The renal corpuscle:

options.label: A
options.text: Has filtration slit-membranes and diaphragms

options.label: B
options.text: Contains mesangial cells, the glomerular filtration barrier and the macula densa

options.label: C
options.text: Contains podocytes and a fused basal lamina

options.label: D
options.text: Consists of the parietal layer, the visceral layer and the vascular endothelium

notes.A: Slit diaphragms bridge filtration slits between adjacent podocyte foot processes and help restrict macromolecules.
notes.B: Mesangial cells and the filtration barrier are within the corpuscle. The macula densa is an adjacent distal tubular structure.
notes.C: Podocyte and endothelial basal laminae contribute to the shared glomerular basement membrane.
notes.D: Bowman’s capsule has an outer parietal epithelium and visceral podocytes over the tuft, whose capillaries have fenestrated endothelium.

questions.why: The renal corpuscle comprises the glomerular capillary tuft and Bowman’s capsule. Its visceral podocytes and capillary endothelium share a basement membrane at the filtration surface.

questions.stem: Specimens A and B were from:

options.label: A
options.text: Urinary bladder and ureter respectively

options.label: B
options.text: Ureter and urinary bladder respectively

options.label: C
options.text: Urinary bladder and urethra respectively

options.label: D
options.text: Urethra and ureter respectively

options.label: E
options.text: Urinary bladder and uterus respectively

questions.why: A: bladder (thick muscle, ill-defined layers). B: ureter (inner longitudinal, outer circular, stellate lumen).

notes.B: Reversed.
notes.C: B is not the urethra.
notes.D: No.
notes.E: No.

questions.stem: The urinary bladder:

options.label: A
options.text: Has a muscularis with three layers of smooth muscle

options.label: B
options.text: Is a distensible reservoir for urine

options.label: C
options.text: Is divided into three parts known as trigones

options.label: D
options.text: Has secretory alveoli and fibromuscular connective tissue

notes.A: The detrusor is conventionally described as three smooth muscle layers, although the bundles interlace and the layers are often indistinct.
notes.B: The bladder expands as urine accumulates. Its urothelium accommodates stretching while maintaining a barrier to urine.
notes.C: There is one trigone, bounded by the two ureteric openings and the internal urethral opening.
notes.D: The bladder has urothelium over a connective tissue layer and detrusor. Secretory alveoli are not a defining bladder feature.

questions.why: The bladder stores urine behind a distensible urothelium. Interlacing detrusor smooth muscle empties the reservoir, and a single smooth triangular trigone lies at its base.

questions.stem: The male urethra has:

options.label: A
options.text: A prostatic part with small prostatic ducts

options.label: B
options.text: A membranous part that is surrounded by striated muscle fibers and lined with stratified or pseudostratified columnar epithelium

options.label: C
options.text: A spongy part, approximately 15cm long, receiving ducts of the bulbourethral glands

options.label: D
options.text: A spongy part that extends through the bulb, body and glans of the penis and lined with transitional epithelium

notes.A: Prostatic ducts open into the prostatic urethra, particularly into grooves beside the urethral crest.
notes.B: The external urethral sphincter surrounds the membranous part, which commonly has pseudostratified or stratified columnar epithelium.
notes.C: The spongy urethra is about fifteen centimetres long. Bulbourethral ducts open into its proximal portion.
notes.D: The spongy part is mostly lined by pseudostratified or stratified columnar epithelium, with more distal squamous lining.

questions.why: The prostatic urethra receives prostatic ducts, the membranous part passes through the striated urethral sphincter, and the spongy part runs within the corpus spongiosum.

questions.stem: The macula densa:

options.label: A
options.text: Is associated with the vascular pole of the glomerulus and is involved in blood pressure regulation

options.label: B
options.text: Monitors blood sodium and lies at the urinary pole of the glomerulus

options.label: C
options.text: Is part of the proximal tubule and makes red blood cells

options.label: D
options.text: Is a portion of the distal tubule that stimulates the Juxtaglomerular cells to secrete renin

options.label: E
options.text: Is a crowding of nuclei in the wall of the distal tubule

notes.A: The macula densa lies at the vascular pole. Its signals help coordinate tubuloglomerular feedback and renin release.
notes.B: It senses sodium chloride in tubular fluid at the vascular pole. The urinary pole is where filtrate enters the proximal tubule.
notes.C: It lies at the end of the thick ascending limb near the distal convoluted tubule and has a sensing role.
notes.D: Reduced luminal sodium chloride promotes signals that stimulate renin secretion by adjacent granular juxtaglomerular cells.
notes.E: Tall, closely spaced cells produce a dense group of nuclei where the distal tubular segment abuts the vascular pole.

questions.why: The macula densa is a cluster of closely packed distal tubular cells at the glomerular vascular pole. It senses luminal sodium chloride and signals to adjust filtration and renin release.

questions.stem: The juxtaglomerular cells:

options.label: A
options.text: Are found in both the proximal and distal convoluted tubules

options.label: B
options.text: Are the source of renin and erythropoietin

options.label: C
options.text: Are modified smooth muscle cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole at the vascular pole

options.label: D
options.text: Have spherical nuclei instead of the typical elongated nuclei of smooth muscle cells and they contain secretory granules

notes.A: Granular cells are in arteriolar walls. The macula densa is the neighbouring specialised distal tubular epithelium.
notes.B: Juxtaglomerular cells release renin. Renal erythropoietin is produced mainly by interstitial cells near peritubular capillaries.
notes.C: The afferent arteriolar media near the glomerulus contains specialised smooth muscle cells with a secretory function.
notes.D: Compared with contractile smooth muscle cells, granular cells have rounder nuclei and cytoplasmic renin granules.

questions.why: Juxtaglomerular cells are modified smooth muscle cells, mainly in the afferent arteriolar wall near the vascular pole. They have rounded nuclei and store renin in granules.

questions.stem: Functions of the kidneys include all of the following EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: The elimination of foreign substances and their breakdown products

options.label: B
options.text: The regulation of total body water

options.label: C
options.text: The maintenance of the extracellular fluid volume

options.label: D
options.text: Synthesis and secretion of renin for control of blood volume

options.label: E
options.text: Secretion of erythropoietin to regulate white blood cell formation

questions.why: The kidney releases erythropoietin in response to reduced oxygen availability. Erythropoietin stimulates red cell production in the bone marrow, while renin helps regulate effective circulating volume.

notes.A: Glomerular filtration and tubular secretion help eliminate many foreign compounds and their metabolites into urine.
notes.B: Adjusting urinary water excretion, including responses to vasopressin, helps regulate total body water.
notes.C: The kidneys regulate sodium excretion and therefore help control extracellular fluid volume over time.
notes.D: Renin initiates the angiotensin cascade, influencing sodium retention, vascular tone and effective circulating volume.

questions.stem: Medullary rays:

options.label: A
options.text: Are part of the cortex and contain projections called renal columns of Bertin

options.label: B
options.text: Consist of renal corpuscles, convoluted portions of the proximal and distal tubules and short lengths of the straight portions of the tubules

options.label: C
options.text: Consist of renal corpuscles, straight portions of the proximal and distal tubules, and short lengths of the Papillary ducts

options.label: D
options.text: Consists of renal corpuscles only

options.label: E
options.text: Contains straight collecting tubules and straight tubule components of the nephron

notes.A: The rays belong to the cortex. Renal columns are separate extensions of cortex between medullary pyramids.
notes.B: Renal corpuscles and convoluted tubules lie in the cortical labyrinth. The rays are formed from straight structures.
notes.C: The rays have straight tubular portions, but renal corpuscles are outside them and papillary ducts open at the papilla.
notes.D: Renal corpuscles lie in the cortical labyrinth. Their presence distinguishes it from the medullary rays.
notes.E: Each ray contains parallel straight portions of nephrons and collecting ducts running between cortex and medulla.

questions.why: Medullary rays are radial bundles within the cortex. They contain straight tubular segments and collecting ducts, while renal corpuscles and convoluted tubules occupy the surrounding cortical labyrinth.

questions.stem: The renal cortex:

options.label: A
options.text: Consists of renal corpuscles, convoluted portions of the proximal and distal tubules and short lengths of the straight portions of the tubules

options.label: B
options.text: Consists of renal corpuscles, straight portions of the proximal and distal tubules, and short lengths of the Papillary ducts

options.label: C
options.text: Consists of renal corpuscles and medullary rays only

options.label: D
options.text: Possess 7-14 minor calyces

notes.A: Cortical labyrinth contains renal corpuscles and convoluted proximal and distal tubules. Straight tubular segments are also present in cortical rays.
notes.B: The collecting ducts merge into papillary ducts near the medullary apex. Papillary ducts are outside the cortex.
notes.C: In addition to corpuscles and medullary rays, the cortex contains abundant proximal and distal convoluted tubules.
notes.D: Minor calyces receive urine at the papillae and lie in the renal sinus, outside the cortical tissue.

questions.why: The renal cortex includes a labyrinth of renal corpuscles and convoluted tubules, interspersed with medullary rays containing straight tubular segments and collecting ducts. Calyces occupy the renal sinus.

questions.stem: A disease caused by inadequate secretion of antidiuretic hormone by the pituitary, with polyuria, is:

options.label: A
options.text: Diabetes mellitus

options.label: B
options.text: Diabetes insipidus

options.label: C
options.text: Diabetic acidosis

options.label: D
options.text: Coma

options.label: E
options.text: Polydipsia

questions.why: A deficiency of vasopressin release from the posterior pituitary causes central diabetes insipidus. Collecting ducts reabsorb less water, leading to large volumes of dilute urine.

notes.A: Diabetes mellitus can cause polyuria through glucose-driven osmotic diuresis. The stem describes a deficiency of vasopressin.
notes.C: Diabetic ketoacidosis involves insulin deficiency and accumulation of ketone bodies. It does not describe impaired vasopressin secretion.
notes.D: Coma is a state of impaired consciousness. It does not identify the endocrine cause of dilute polyuria.
notes.E: Polydipsia describes increased thirst and can follow urinary water loss. It does not name the condition caused by low vasopressin.

questions.stem: Select the correct statement about nephrons.

options.label: A
options.text: The parietal layer of the glomerular capsule is simple squamous epithelium

options.label: B
options.text: The glomerulus is the proximal end of the proximal convoluted tubule

options.label: C
options.text: Podocytes are branching cells that line the tubules

options.label: D
options.text: Filtration slits are the pores of fenestrated capillaries

options.label: E
options.text: Podocytes are cuboidal cells lining the tubules

questions.why: The parietal layer of Bowman’s capsule is simple squamous epithelium. Visceral podocytes cover the glomerular capillaries, and the capsule continues into the proximal tubule at the urinary pole.

notes.B: The glomerulus is a capillary tuft inside Bowman’s capsule. The proximal convoluted tubule begins at the urinary pole.
notes.C: Podocytes are branching epithelial cells that cover glomerular capillaries. They do not line the nephron’s tubules.
notes.D: Filtration slits lie between podocyte foot processes. Endothelial fenestrations are separate openings in the capillary lining.
notes.E: The proximal tubule is lined by specialised cuboidal cells. Podocytes form the covering of the glomerular tuft.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus?

options.label: A
options.text: Juxtaglomerular (granular) cells

options.label: B
options.text: Macula densa

options.label: C
options.text: Podocytes

options.label: D
options.text: Extraglomerular mesangial cells

options.label: E
options.text: Lacis cells

questions.why: The juxtaglomerular apparatus includes distal tubular macula densa cells, arteriolar granular cells and extraglomerular mesangial cells. Podocytes cover glomerular capillaries and help form the filtration barrier.

notes.A: Granular cells store and release renin and are found mainly in the afferent arteriolar wall near the vascular pole.
notes.B: The macula densa senses tubular sodium chloride and signals to neighbouring cells at the vascular pole.
notes.D: Extraglomerular mesangial cells lie between the distal tubule and the glomerular arterioles and form part of the apparatus.
notes.E: Lacis cells are another name for extraglomerular mesangial cells, a component of the juxtaglomerular apparatus.

questions.stem: Each of the following is part of the urinary system EXCEPT the:

options.label: A
options.text: Kidney

options.label: B
options.text: Urinary bladder

options.label: C
options.text: Rectum

options.label: D
options.text: Ureter

options.label: E
options.text: Urethra

questions.why: The urinary system forms, transports, stores and expels urine through the kidneys, ureters, bladder and urethra. The rectum is a terminal portion of the digestive tract.

notes.A: The kidneys filter plasma and adjust the filtrate to produce urine, so they are urinary organs.
notes.B: The bladder stores urine delivered by the ureters and empties it into the urethra during voiding.
notes.D: The ureter carries urine from the renal pelvis to the urinary bladder by smooth muscle peristalsis.
notes.E: The urethra carries urine from the bladder to the exterior and is the final urinary passage.

questions.stem: The triangular (conical) structures in the renal medulla are the:

options.label: A
options.text: Pyramids

options.label: B
options.text: Renal columns

options.label: C
options.text: Renal pelvises

options.label: D
options.text: Nephrons

options.label: E
options.text: Calyces

questions.why: Renal pyramids are conical medullary regions containing parallel tubules and ducts. The base faces the cortex, and the tip forms a papilla projecting into a minor calyx.

notes.B: Renal columns are extensions of cortical tissue between neighbouring medullary pyramids rather than the conical medullary structures.
notes.C: The renal pelvis is the funnel-shaped common collecting space in the sinus that continues into the ureter.
notes.D: Nephrons are microscopic filtration and tubular units. Many of their tubular segments contribute to each pyramid.
notes.E: Calyces are collecting spaces that receive urine from the papillae. They are separate from the medullary tissue.

questions.stem: The expanded upper end of the ureter is the:

options.label: A
options.text: Renal sinus

options.label: B
options.text: Renal pelvis

options.label: C
options.text: Major calyx

options.label: D
options.text: Minor calyx

options.label: E
options.text: Renal corpuscle

questions.why: The renal pelvis is the funnel-shaped expansion continuous with the proximal ureter. It collects urine from the major calyces and channels it into the ureter.

notes.A: The renal sinus is a cavity containing calyces, the renal pelvis, vessels and fat. It is larger than the collecting lumen.
notes.C: A major calyx joins multiple minor calyces and carries urine into the pelvis upstream of the ureter.
notes.D: A minor calyx is a small cup that receives urine at a renal papilla and empties into a major calyx.
notes.E: The renal corpuscle is the microscopic filtration unit formed by glomerular capillaries and Bowman’s capsule.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a function of the kidney?

options.label: A
options.text: Control of total water

options.label: B
options.text: Control of the electrolyte composition of the blood

options.label: C
options.text: Excretion of excess albumin

options.label: D
options.text: Control of production of red blood cells by bone marrow

options.label: E
options.text: Regulation of blood pressure

questions.why: The glomerular filtration barrier restricts most circulating albumin, and the proximal tubule retrieves much of the small amount that passes. Eliminating excess albumin is not a normal renal regulatory function.

notes.A: Kidneys adjust water excretion in response to changes in body water and vasopressin, helping maintain osmolality.
notes.B: Renal tubular reabsorption and secretion help control the concentrations of electrolytes such as sodium and potassium.
notes.D: The kidneys make erythropoietin in response to reduced oxygen availability. It stimulates bone marrow red cell production.
notes.E: Regulation of sodium and water balance, together with renin release, helps control arterial blood pressure.

questions.stem: Filtrate passes from the glomerular capsule first into the:

options.label: A
options.text: Nephron loop (loop of Henle)

options.label: B
options.text: Proximal convoluted tubule

options.label: C
options.text: Distal convoluted tubule

options.label: D
options.text: Collecting duct

options.label: E
options.text: Minor calyx

questions.why: At the urinary pole of Bowman’s capsule, filtrate enters the proximal convoluted tubule. Its brush border provides surface area for the first stage of bulk reabsorption.

notes.A: The nephron loop receives filtrate after it has passed through the proximal convoluted and straight tubular segments.
notes.C: The distal convoluted tubule receives fluid after it has passed through the loop of Henle.
notes.D: The collecting duct receives tubular fluid after passage through the distal nephron and connecting segment.
notes.E: A minor calyx receives urine from papillary ducts, after the filtrate has traversed the nephron and collecting system.

questions.stem: The part of the nephron that empties into the collecting duct is the:

options.label: A
options.text: Nephron loop (loop of Henle)

options.label: B
options.text: Proximal convoluted tubule

options.label: C
options.text: Distal convoluted tubule

options.label: D
options.text: Papillary tubule

options.label: E
options.text: Minor calyx

questions.why: The distal convoluted tubule is the last nephron segment listed before the collecting system. Its outflow passes through a short connecting tubule to reach a collecting duct.

notes.A: The nephron loop returns fluid to the cortex and leads to the distal convoluted tubule upstream of the collecting system.
notes.B: The proximal convoluted tubule begins at Bowman’s capsule and leads to the straight proximal segment.
notes.D: A papillary duct receives fluid downstream from converging collecting ducts and opens at the papilla.
notes.E: The minor calyx receives urine from papillary ducts after it has left the microscopic collecting system.

questions.stem: The primary function of the proximal convoluted tubule is

options.label: A
options.text: Filtration

options.label: B
options.text: Absorption of ions, organic molecules, vitamins, and water

options.label: C
options.text: Secretion of acids and ammonia

options.label: D
options.text: Secretion of drugs

options.label: E
options.text: Adjusting the urine volume

questions.why: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs most filtered sodium and water, along with nearly all filtered glucose and amino acids at normal plasma concentrations. Its brush border increases transport area.

notes.A: Filtration occurs across the glomerular barrier. The proximal tubule receives the filtrate after it enters Bowman’s space.
notes.C: The proximal tubule contributes to acid handling and produces ammonium, but bulk reabsorption accounts for most of its transport.
notes.D: Proximal tubular cells secrete some drugs into the lumen. This is a secondary role alongside large-volume reabsorption.
notes.E: The proximal tubule reabsorbs water in bulk, and collecting duct water permeability provides the main final adjustment of urine volume.

questions.stem: Vessels: 1 afferent arteriole, 2 arcuate artery, 3 interlobar artery, 4 renal artery, 5 glomerulus, 6 cortical radiate artery, 7 efferent arteriole, 8 peritubular capillaries. The order in which blood passes through them is:
questions.why: Renal arterial branches lead from interlobar to arcuate and cortical radiate vessels. An afferent arteriole supplies each glomerulus, and its efferent arteriole feeds a downstream capillary bed.

notes.A: Branches proceed from interlobar to arcuate to cortical radiate arteries. Cortical radiate arteries therefore come after the arcuate branches.
notes.C: The afferent arteriole carries blood into the glomerular capillaries. The efferent arteriole carries it away.
notes.D: Cortical radiate arteries arise from arcuate arteries, and the afferent arteriole is upstream of the glomerulus.
notes.E: Interlobar arteries give rise to arcuate arteries at the pyramid bases. Cortical radiate branches follow from there.

questions.stem: The filtration barrier of the renal corpuscle consists of:

options.label: A
options.text: Filtration slits, foot processes and slit pores

options.label: B
options.text: Fenestrations, mesangial matrix and foot processes

options.label: C
options.text: Fenestrated endothelium, glomerular basement membrane and podocyte filtration slits

options.label: D
options.text: Basement membrane, foot processes and fenestrations of the capsule

options.label: E
options.text: Podocyte filtration slits, mesangium and the parietal layer

questions.why: Water and small solutes cross fenestrated endothelium, the shared glomerular basement membrane and slit diaphragms between podocyte processes. Together these layers limit the passage of blood cells and large proteins.

notes.A: Foot processes and the slits between them are components of the podocyte layer. Endothelium and basement membrane are also required.
notes.B: Mesangial matrix supports capillary loops within the tuft. It is separate from the basement membrane on the filtration path.
notes.D: The fenestrations are in the glomerular capillary endothelium. The parietal wall of Bowman’s capsule is outside the barrier.
notes.E: The visceral podocytes form the epithelial layer of the barrier. The parietal layer and mesangium are not serial filtration layers.

questions.stem: Sympathetic stimulation of the kidney can do all of the following, except

options.label: A
options.text: Produce powerful vasoconstriction of the afferent arterioles

options.label: B
options.text: Increase the glomerular filtration rate

options.label: C
options.text: Trigger renin release

options.label: D
options.text: Produce renal ischemia

options.label: E
options.text: Both B and C

questions.why: Strong renal sympathetic stimulation constricts renal arterioles, reducing renal blood flow and usually lowering filtration. It also promotes renin release through beta-1 receptors on granular cells.

notes.A: Sympathetic alpha-adrenergic signalling constricts afferent arterioles, particularly when activation is strong.
notes.C: Beta-1 stimulation of juxtaglomerular granular cells promotes renin release as part of the volume-preserving response.
notes.D: A marked fall in renal perfusion can produce ischaemia when sympathetic vasoconstriction is severe.
notes.E: Increased filtration is the exception. The additional claim about renin release describes an established sympathetic response.

questions.stem: Which of the following descriptions best matches the term loop of Henle?

options.label: A
options.text: Relies on countercurrent multiplication

options.label: B
options.text: Creates a high interstitial NaCl concentration

options.label: C
options.text: Enables production of hypertonic urine

options.label: D
options.text: A, B and C

options.label: E
options.text: B and C only

questions.why: The loop of Henle multiplies an osmotic gradient along the medulla. Salt transport in the ascending limb helps build that gradient, allowing vasopressin-sensitive collecting ducts to conserve water.

notes.A: Countercurrent multiplication does occur, and the single mechanism leaves out the resulting gradient and ability to concentrate urine.
notes.B: The loop does increase interstitial sodium chloride, but this describes only the salt-gradient part of its role.
notes.C: The medullary gradient helps support hypertonic urine when ducts are water permeable. This is one consequence of the mechanism.
notes.E: Both effects are valid, and the combination leaves out countercurrent multiplication that establishes the gradient.

questions.stem: The ureters and urinary bladder are lined by

options.label: A
options.text: Stratified squamous epithelium

options.label: B
options.text: Pseudostratified columnar epithelium

options.label: C
options.text: Simple cuboidal epithelium

options.label: D
options.text: Transitional epithelium

options.label: E
options.text: Simple columnar epithelium

questions.why: The ureter and bladder are lined by urothelium, also called transitional epithelium. Its superficial umbrella cells flatten with distension and maintain a barrier against urine.

notes.A: Stratified squamous epithelium protects surfaces such as the distal urethral opening. The ureter and bladder have specialised urothelium.
notes.B: Pseudostratified columnar epithelium can occur in the urethra. The ureter and bladder lining has multiple layers with umbrella cells.
notes.C: Simple cuboidal epithelium lines many renal tubules. The ureter and bladder require a stretchable stratified lining.
notes.E: Simple columnar epithelium lines much of the gut. Urothelium has several layers adapted to distension.

questions.stem: The detrusor muscle

options.label: A
options.text: Moves urine along the ureters by peristalsis

options.label: B
options.text: Compresses the bladder and expels urine through the urethra

options.label: C
options.text: Functions as the internal urinary sphincter

options.label: D
options.text: Functions as the external urinary sphincter

options.label: E
options.text: Surrounds the renal pelvis

questions.why: The detrusor is the smooth muscle coat of the bladder. When it contracts during micturition, it raises intravesical pressure as outlet resistance falls, expelling urine.

notes.A: Smooth muscle in the ureter wall generates peristalsis. The detrusor is located in the bladder wall.
notes.C: Smooth muscle at the bladder neck helps control the outlet. The detrusor provides the pressure for bladder emptying.
notes.D: The external urethral sphincter is striated muscle. Detrusor smooth muscle contracts involuntarily during voiding.
notes.E: The renal pelvis has its own smooth muscle to help propel urine. Detrusor is the muscle coat of the bladder.

questions.stem: In response to increased levels of aldosterone, the kidneys produce

options.label: A
options.text: A larger volume of urine

options.label: B
options.text: Urine with a higher concentration of sodium ions

options.label: C
options.text: Urine with a lower concentration of potassium ions

options.label: D
options.text: Urine with a lower concentration of sodium ions

options.label: E
options.text: Urine with less glucose

questions.why: Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion.

notes.A: Less urine.
notes.B: Lower sodium.
notes.C: Higher potassium.
notes.E: No effect.

questions.stem: An inflammatory disorder of the glomeruli that affects filtration is:

options.label: A
options.text: Glomerulonephritis

options.label: B
options.text: Floating kidney

options.label: C
options.text: Polycystic kidney disease

options.label: D
options.text: Pyelonephrosis

options.label: E
options.text: Kidney stones

questions.why: Glomerulonephritis involves inflammation or immune-mediated injury of glomeruli. Damage to their filtration barrier can allow blood or protein into urine, and filtration rate can fall.

notes.B: A floating kidney is an abnormally mobile kidney, also called nephroptosis. It is not a primary glomerular inflammatory disorder.
notes.C: Polycystic kidney disease produces numerous fluid-filled cysts, which distort renal tissue as they enlarge.
notes.D: Pyelonephrosis is a term for disease of the renal pelvis and kidney. Inflammation centred on the glomeruli is glomerulonephritis.
notes.E: Kidney stones are concretions within the urinary tract. They can obstruct urine flow but do not define glomerular inflammation.

questions.stem: Renal blood flow is about:

options.label: A
options.text: 1 liter/min

options.label: B
options.text: 2 liter/min

options.label: C
options.text: 3 liter/min

options.label: D
options.text: 4 liter/min

options.label: E
options.text: 5 liter/min

questions.why: At rest the kidneys receive roughly one-fifth of cardiac output, about 1 to 1.2 litres of blood per minute in a typical adult. This flow supports filtration and solute regulation.

notes.B: Two litres per minute would represent nearly half of a typical resting cardiac output, above the usual renal share.
notes.C: Three litres per minute would account for most resting cardiac output. The kidneys normally receive about one-fifth.
notes.D: Four litres per minute approaches the total resting cardiac output of a small adult and exceeds typical renal blood flow.
notes.E: Five litres per minute is close to typical total resting cardiac output. The kidneys receive only a fraction of it.

questions.stem: An increase in the permeability of the cells of the collecting tubule to water is due to a(n)

options.label: A
options.text: Decrease in the production of ADH

options.label: B
options.text: Increase in the production of ADH

options.label: C
options.text: Increase in the production of aldosterone

options.label: D
options.text: Decrease in the concentration of the blood plasma

options.label: E
options.text: Increase in the production of ACTH

questions.why: Vasopressin activates V2 receptors on collecting duct principal cells, increasing apical aquaporin-2 channels. The higher water permeability lets water leave tubular fluid along the medullary osmotic gradient.

notes.A: A fall in vasopressin reduces apical aquaporin-2 abundance and decreases collecting duct water reabsorption.
notes.C: Aldosterone chiefly stimulates sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion. Vasopressin is the direct regulator of apical aquaporin-2 insertion.
notes.D: A fall in plasma osmolality normally suppresses vasopressin release, reducing collecting duct water permeability.
notes.E: ACTH acts mainly on the adrenal cortex to stimulate glucocorticoid production. It does not directly insert collecting duct water channels.

questions.stem: The descending limb of the loop of Henle

options.label: A
options.text: Is not permeable to water

options.label: B
options.text: Is freely permeable to sodium and urea

options.label: C
options.text: Pulls water by osmosis into the lumen of the tubule

options.label: D
options.text: Contains fluid that becomes more concentrated as it descends into the medulla

options.label: E
options.text: Contains fluid that becomes less concentrated as it descends into the medulla

questions.why: In water-permeable portions of the thin descending limb, water moves into the hyperosmotic medullary interstitium. This leaves progressively more concentrated tubular fluid on the way down.

notes.A: Much of the thin descending limb has high water permeability. The ascending limb has low water permeability.
notes.B: Solute permeability varies with the segment. The characteristic response in water-permeable descending segments is osmotic water loss.
notes.C: The more concentrated medullary interstitium draws water out of the descending limb by osmosis.
notes.E: Net water movement out of the tubule raises luminal concentration as fluid descends through the medulla.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT associated with the renal corpuscle?

options.label: A
options.text: A podocyte

options.label: B
options.text: A vasa recta

options.label: C
options.text: A fenestrated capillary
