options.label: D
options.text: An efferent arteriole

options.label: E
options.text: Parietal layer of the renal capsule

questions.why: Vasa recta are medullary capillaries from efferent arterioles of juxtamedullary nephrons.

notes.A: Visceral layer.
notes.C: Glomerular capillary.
notes.D: Drains it.
notes.E: Part.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the structure of the ureters?

options.label: A
options.text: They have three coats: mucosa, muscularis and adventitia

options.label: B
options.text: They are an extension of the visceral peritoneum

options.label: C
options.text: They are made of several layers of endothelium

options.label: D
options.text: They are made entirely of muscle

options.label: E
options.text: Their muscularis is inner circular and outer longitudinal

questions.why: The ureter wall consists of a urothelial mucosa, smooth muscle muscularis and outer adventitia. The muscularis propels urine by peristalsis, and the adventitia anchors the ureter to adjacent tissue.

notes.B: The ureter is largely retroperitoneal, with an outer connective tissue adventitia. It is separate from the visceral peritoneum.
notes.C: Urothelium lines the lumen, and endothelium is found in vessels supplying the wall.
notes.D: The smooth muscle coat is one part of the wall. The ureter also has a mucosa and an adventitia.
notes.E: In the upper ureter, muscle is generally inner longitudinal and outer circular. An outer longitudinal layer is added distally.

questions.stem: Which statement about the male urethra is FALSE?

options.label: A
options.text: It carries urine and semen at the same time

options.label: B
options.text: It serves the urinary and reproductive systems at different times

options.label: C
options.text: It is longer than the female urethra

options.label: D
options.text: It is a passage for both urine and semen

options.label: E
options.text: It is lined mainly by stratified or pseudostratified columnar epithelium

questions.why: The male urethra is a shared outlet for urine and semen during separate physiological processes. Closure at the bladder neck during ejaculation helps direct semen outward.

notes.B: The urethra serves both systems, but ejaculation and urinary voiding are normally coordinated as distinct events.
notes.C: The male urethra passes through the prostate, pelvic outlet and penis, making it longer than the female urethra.
notes.D: The same urethral channel carries urine during voiding and semen during ejaculation.
notes.E: Much of the male urethra has pseudostratified or stratified columnar lining, with urothelium proximally and squamous epithelium distally.

questions.stem: Which is NOT reabsorbed by the proximal convoluted tubule?

options.label: A
options.text: Na⁺

options.label: B
options.text: K⁺

options.label: C
options.text: Glucose

options.label: D
options.text: Creatinine

options.label: E
options.text: Water

questions.why: Creatinine passes through the glomerular filter and a small amount is secreted by proximal tubular cells. Negligible reabsorption distinguishes it from sodium, potassium, glucose and water.

notes.A: Proximal sodium transport reabsorbs a large fraction of the filtered sodium load and helps drive solute and water reabsorption.
notes.B: A substantial fraction of filtered potassium is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, largely via the paracellular pathway.
notes.C: Sodium-glucose cotransport reabsorbs almost all filtered glucose at normal plasma concentrations.
notes.E: Water follows solutes osmotically, so the proximal tubule reabsorbs much of the filtered water.

questions.stem: The renal sinus is

options.label: A
options.text: The innermost layer of kidney tissue

options.label: B
options.text: Part of a renal pyramid

options.label: C
options.text: An internal cavity lined by the fibrous capsule

options.label: D
options.text: A large branch of the renal pelvis

options.label: E
options.text: A renal corpuscle

questions.why: The renal sinus is the cavity inside the kidney, continuous with the hilum and lined by the fibrous capsule, holding the pelvis, calyces, vessels and fat.

notes.A: Medulla.
notes.B: Pyramids are medulla, not the sinus.
notes.D: Calyx.
notes.E: A renal corpuscle is a microscopic filtering unit.

questions.stem: The renal myofibroblasts are

options.label: A
options.text: Located in the inner part of the renal capsule

options.label: B
options.text: Smooth muscle-like cells

options.label: C
options.text: Cells with contractile elements that resist the volume and pressure beds in the kidney

options.label: D
options.text: A and C are correct

options.label: E
options.text: A, B and C are correct

questions.why: Myofibroblasts in the inner capsule are contractile, smooth-muscle-like cells.

notes.A: True.
notes.B: True.
notes.C: True.
notes.D: B is also true.

questions.stem: Renal columns are

options.label: A
options.text: Internal cavities lined by the fibrous capsule

options.label: B
options.text: Expanded ends of the ureters

options.label: C
options.text: The basic functional units of the kidney

options.label: D
options.text: Bands of cortical tissue extending between the pyramids

options.label: E
options.text: Conical structures that are located in the renal medulla

questions.why: Renal columns are bands of cortical tissue between neighbouring medullary pyramids. Interlobar vessels pass through these columns towards the base of each pyramid at the corticomedullary junction.

notes.A: The renal sinus is an internal cavity at the hilum. A renal column is solid cortical tissue between pyramids.
notes.B: The renal pelvis is the expanded proximal end of the ureter and receives urine from major calyces.
notes.C: A nephron is a functional unit made of a renal corpuscle and tubule. A column is a larger anatomical region.
notes.E: The conical structures in the medulla are renal pyramids. Cortical columns extend into the spaces between pyramids.

questions.stem: Major calyces are

options.label: A
options.text: Large branches of the renal pelvis

options.label: B
options.text: Expanded ends of nephrons

options.label: C
options.text: Basic functional layers of the kidney

options.label: D
options.text: Conical structures that are located in the renal medulla

options.label: E
options.text: The expanded ends of renal pyramids

questions.why: Several minor calyces usually unite to form each major calyx. The major calyces drain into the renal pelvis, which funnels urine toward the proximal ureter.

notes.B: A nephron has a renal corpuscle and a tubular portion. Its terminal tubular fluid reaches a collecting duct.
notes.C: The renal cortex and medulla are the main tissue regions. Calyces are parts of the urine collecting system.
notes.D: Renal pyramids are cones of medullary tissue. They discharge urine into calyces through ducts opening at the papillae.
notes.E: The terminal tip of a renal pyramid is the papilla, which projects into a minor calyx.

questions.stem: The ability to form a concentrated urine depends on the functions of

options.label: A
options.text: The proximal convoluted tubule

options.label: B
options.text: The distal convoluted tubule

options.label: C
options.text: The collecting duct

options.label: D
options.text: The loop of Henle

options.label: E
options.text: Both C and D

questions.why: The loop of Henle establishes the medullary osmotic gradient. With vasopressin, the collecting ducts become water permeable and use this gradient to produce urine more concentrated than plasma.

notes.A: Bulk water and solute reabsorption takes place in the proximal tubule, where tubular fluid is normally close to plasma osmolality.
notes.B: The distal convoluted tubule reabsorbs salt and helps dilute tubular fluid. Final water recovery occurs mainly farther downstream.
notes.C: The collecting duct is where vasopressin increases water recovery. This relies on a gradient built in part by the loop.
notes.D: The loop establishes the gradient, but the collecting duct must be water permeable for the final urine to concentrate.

questions.stem: The part of the uriniferous tubule whose cells have the longest microvilli, abundant lateral plications, basal interdigitations and most mitochondria is the:

options.label: A
options.text: Glomerular capsular podocytes

options.label: B
options.text: Proximal convoluted tubule of the nephron

options.label: C
options.text: Thin segment of the loop of Henle

options.label: D
options.text: Distal tubule

options.label: E
options.text: Distal convoluted tubule

questions.why: Proximal convoluted tubule cells have a tall apical brush border, folded basolateral surfaces and abundant mitochondria. These adaptations provide membrane area and energy for high rates of reabsorption.

notes.A: Podocytes have branching foot processes and slit diaphragms for filtration. They do not have a tall absorptive brush border.
notes.C: Thin limb cells form a flat simple squamous lining with far less cytoplasm than proximal tubular cells.
notes.D: Distal tubular cells can have substantial basolateral folding but lack the tall, dense proximal brush border.
notes.E: The distal convoluted tubule has shorter and sparser apical microvilli, so its lumen looks clearer in sections.

questions.stem: Parts of the uriniferous tubule that do NOT have simple cuboidal epithelium are the:

options.label: A
options.text: Proximal and distal convoluted tubules

options.label: B
options.text: Parietal layer of the glomerular capsule and the thin segment of the loop of Henle

options.label: C
options.text: Glomerular capsular podocyte layer and thick descending limb of the loop of Henle

options.label: D
options.text: Proximal convoluted tubules and collecting tubules

options.label: E
options.text: Collecting tubules and thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

questions.why: Both the parietal layer of Bowman’s capsule and the thin limb of Henle have flattened simple squamous cells. Thick tubular segments generally have simple cuboidal epithelium.

notes.A: Both convoluted tubules have simple cuboidal epithelium. The proximal one has a more prominent brush border.
notes.C: The visceral layer has podocytes, but the thick descending portion is the cuboidal proximal straight tubule.
notes.D: Proximal convoluted tubules and smaller collecting tubules have cuboidal cells. Larger collecting ducts become more columnar.
notes.E: The thick ascending limb and smaller collecting tubules generally have cuboidal lining, although their cells differ in function.

questions.stem: The main function of the transitional epithelium in the ureter is:

options.label: A
options.text: The secretion of mucus to protect the excretory passages

options.label: B
options.text: Not the same as that of the transitional epithelium lining the urinary bladder

options.label: C
options.text: Protection against kidney stones

options.label: D
options.text: Reabsorption and protection against renal calculi

options.label: E
options.text: Stretching and impermeablity to water and salt

questions.why: Ureteric urothelium stretches as urine passes. Its superficial umbrella cells, tight junctions and surface plaques maintain a high-resistance barrier to water and solute movement.

notes.A: Surface plaques and tight junctions provide the main barrier. Mucus secretion is not the defining role of ureteric urothelium.
notes.B: Urothelium is the lining of both the ureter and bladder, where it combines distensibility with low permeability.
notes.C: Stones can injure the lining. The usual role of urothelium is to provide a flexible barrier to urine.
notes.D: Reabsorption is a function of renal tubular epithelium. The ureter transports urine without substantially changing its composition.

questions.stem: A major function of the collecting tubules is:

options.label: A
options.text: Secretion and filtration

options.label: B
options.text: Filtration and concentrating urine

options.label: C
options.text: Concentrating urine

options.label: D
options.text: Secretion and lubrication with mucus

options.label: E
options.text: Stretching and secretion

questions.why: Collecting tubules vary their water permeability in response to vasopressin. When permeability increases, water leaves into the hyperosmotic medulla and the remaining fluid becomes more concentrated.

notes.A: Collecting tubules can secrete ions, but filtration occurs in glomerular capillaries upstream in the nephron.
notes.B: The collecting system helps concentrate urine, while filtration takes place separately across the glomerular barrier.
notes.D: Collecting tubules regulate water and ion handling. They do not have a mucous lining for lubrication.
notes.E: Stretchable urothelium lines structures such as the ureter and bladder, whereas collecting tubules have cells specialised for transport.

questions.stem: The cavity of the kidney that receives urine from the calyces is called the

options.label: A
options.text: Renal papilla

options.label: B
options.text: Renal pelvis

options.label: C
options.text: Renal medulla

options.label: D
options.text: Renal cortex

options.label: E
options.text: Renal sinus

questions.why: Major calyces empty into the renal pelvis, the funnel-shaped collecting lumen within the renal sinus. The pelvis narrows as it becomes continuous with the ureter.

notes.A: A papilla is the tip of a renal pyramid. Papillary ducts release urine into the surrounding minor calyx.
notes.C: The renal medulla is parenchyma containing tubules and collecting ducts. It is not the hollow collector that receives the calyces.
notes.D: The renal cortex contains corpuscles and tubules. The collecting cavity described lies centrally within the sinus.
notes.E: The sinus contains the pelvis, calyces, vessels and fat. Only the lumen of the pelvis receives urine from major calyces.

questions.stem: Changes that occur in the urinary system with aging include all of the following, except <

options.label: A
options.text: A decline in the number of functional nephrons

options.label: B
options.text: A reduction in the GFR (glomerular filtration rate)

options.label: C
options.text: Increased sensitivity to ADH

options.label: D
options.text: Problems with the micturition reflex

options.label: E
options.text: Loss of sphincter muscle tonus

questions.why: Ageing can reduce functional nephron number, glomerular filtration and maximum urine concentrating ability. The older kidney’s concentrating response to vasopressin is often blunted, even when hormone secretion is preserved.

notes.A: Functional nephron number can fall with age because of nephron loss and increasing glomerulosclerosis.
notes.B: Measured glomerular filtration commonly falls with age, although the rate and extent vary between individuals.
notes.D: Age-related changes in bladder sensation, neural control or detrusor function can alter the voiding reflex.
notes.E: Urethral closure pressure and sphincter function can decline with age, contributing to urinary leakage in some people.

questions.stem: Which delivers urine to a minor calyx?

options.label: A
options.text: Nephron loop (loop of Henle)

options.label: B
options.text: Distal convoluted tubule

options.label: C
options.text: Papillary duct

options.label: D
options.text: Renal corpuscle

options.label: E
options.text: Ureter

questions.why: Collecting ducts converge to form papillary ducts of Bellini. These ducts open at the tip of a renal pyramid, where a minor calyx receives the urine.

notes.A: The loop of Henle passes tubular fluid to the distal nephron before it enters the collecting system.
notes.B: The distal convoluted tubule delivers fluid toward the connecting tubule and collecting duct, upstream of papillary drainage.
notes.D: Plasma filtration occurs in the renal corpuscle, and the filtrate first passes into the proximal tubule.
notes.E: The ureter carries urine from the renal pelvis to the bladder, downstream of both minor and major calyces.

questions.stem: The filtration of plasma takes place in the

options.label: A
options.text: Nephron loop (loop of Henle)

options.label: B
options.text: Distal convoluted tubule

options.label: C
options.text: Papillary duct

options.label: D
options.text: Renal corpuscle

options.label: E
options.text: Ureter

questions.why: Plasma filtration occurs in the renal corpuscle. Hydrostatic pressure drives water and small solutes across glomerular capillary walls and podocyte slit diaphragms into Bowman’s space.

notes.A: The loop of Henle has tubular segments that transport water and solutes after the filtrate has already formed.
notes.B: The distal convoluted tubule adjusts electrolyte content by transport across its epithelium. It receives existing filtrate.
notes.C: A papillary duct carries the final tubular fluid to a minor calyx. It is downstream of the filtration site.
notes.E: The ureter transports urine to the bladder by peristalsis. Its urothelium forms a barrier and has no plasma filtration role.

questions.stem: Besides removing wastes, the kidneys help regulate:

options.label: A
options.text: Blood volume

options.label: B
options.text: Blood pH

options.label: C
options.text: Blood pressure

options.label: D
options.text: Blood ion levels

options.label: E
options.text: All of the above

questions.why: The kidneys vary sodium, water, acid and electrolyte excretion to maintain the internal environment. Volume control and the renin–angiotensin system also help regulate arterial pressure.

notes.A: The kidneys adjust sodium and water excretion to help maintain the extracellular fluid and circulating blood volumes.
notes.B: Net acid excretion and bicarbonate reclamation help keep blood pH within its normal range.
notes.C: Renal sodium handling and renin release influence circulating volume and vascular tone, respectively helping regulate arterial pressure.
notes.D: Variable tubular transport helps keep plasma concentrations of sodium, potassium and other ions within physiological limits.

questions.stem: An inability of the kidneys to excrete adequately to maintain homeostasis is

options.label: A
options.text: Glomerulonephritis

options.label: B
options.text: Polycystic kidney disease

options.label: C
options.text: Calculi

options.label: D
options.text: Renal failure

options.label: E
options.text: Hematuria

questions.why: Renal failure is a loss of kidney function severe enough to impair waste excretion and control of fluid, electrolytes or acid–base balance. It can develop acutely or chronically.

notes.A: Glomerulonephritis is a cause of glomerular injury that can impair filtration. The stem describes the resulting functional state generally.
notes.B: Polycystic kidney disease causes expanding renal cysts and can eventually reduce function. It describes a specific cause.
notes.C: Calculi are urinary stones. They can obstruct flow and damage renal function but are not the general functional diagnosis.
notes.E: Haematuria refers to blood in urine and can occur even when overall excretory function is preserved.

questions.stem: About what percentage of the filtrate is reabsorbed as it passes through the renal tubules?
questions.why: An adult filters roughly 180 litres of fluid per day but typically excretes only about one to two litres. Net tubular reabsorption therefore returns roughly 99 percent to the circulation.

notes.A: One percent is approximately the fraction of filtered water normally excreted, leaving almost all to be reabsorbed.
notes.B: If only 38 percent were recovered, most of the filtered water would be lost. Normal daily urine volume is far lower.
notes.C: This is near the fraction that may be reabsorbed in the proximal tubule alone. Further reabsorption occurs downstream.
notes.D: Recovery continues after the proximal tubule. Reabsorbing only about three-quarters overall would leave far more than a normal urine volume.

questions.stem: Urine passes, in the order given, through which of the following structures?

options.label: A
options.text: Collecting duct, renal pelvis, urethra, bladder, ureter

options.label: B
options.text: Renal pelvis, collecting duct, bladder, ureter, urethra

options.label: C
options.text: Collecting duct, renal pelvis, ureter, bladder, urethra

options.label: D
options.text: Renal pelvis, urethra, bladder, ureter, collecting duct

options.label: E
options.text: Collecting duct, ureter, renal pelvis, urethra, bladder

questions.why: Collecting ducts empty through papillary ducts into the calyces, which drain into the renal pelvis. The ureter then carries urine to the bladder and the urethra carries it outside.

notes.A: The ureter carries urine from the renal pelvis to the bladder. The urethra is the final passage after the bladder.
notes.B: The collecting ducts reach the calyces before the renal pelvis. The bladder receives urine through the ureters.
notes.D: The collecting duct is upstream of the renal pelvis. The urethra is the final outlet downstream of the bladder.
notes.E: The renal pelvis drains into the ureter. From there urine passes to the bladder and then through the urethra.

questions.stem: In the kidney majority of glomeruli are located in the

options.label: A
options.text: Vasa recta

options.label: B
options.text: Medulla

options.label: C
options.text: Cortex

options.label: D
options.text: Pelvis

options.label: E
options.text: Calyces

questions.why: Renal corpuscles all lie in the cortex, including those near the corticomedullary junction. The medulla contains tubular and vascular structures such as loops, collecting ducts and vasa recta.

notes.A: Vasa recta are medullary capillaries derived from efferent arterioles of juxtamedullary nephrons, not sites containing glomeruli.
notes.B: Even juxtamedullary renal corpuscles are on the cortical side of the junction. Their long tubular loops descend into the medulla.
notes.D: The renal pelvis is the funnel-shaped lumen that receives urine from major calyces. It contains no renal corpuscles.
notes.E: Calyces are urine-collecting spaces around papillae and have a urothelial lining. The filtering tufts are within renal cortex.

questions.stem: Urine passes from the:

options.label: A
options.text: Renal hilum to the urinary bladder to the ureter

options.label: B
options.text: Pelvis of the kidney to ureter to urinary bladder to urethra

options.label: C
options.text: Glomerulus to ureter to renal tubule

options.label: D
options.text: Hilum to urethra to urinary bladder

options.label: E
options.text: Renal pelvis to major calyx to minor calyx to urinary bladder

questions.why: Urine leaves the renal pelvis through a ureter and enters the bladder for storage. During voiding it exits through the urethra to the exterior.

notes.A: The ureter passes out through the renal hilum and carries urine to the bladder. Its flow is toward the bladder.
notes.C: Glomerular filtration produces fluid entering Bowman’s space. It then passes through renal tubules before reaching the ureter.
notes.D: The urethra follows the bladder and carries urine outside. Urine approaches the bladder through the ureter.
notes.E: Minor calyces drain into major calyces and the pelvis. From the pelvis, the next passage is the ureter.

questions.stem: The renal corpuscle is made up of

options.label: A
options.text: Bowman's capsule and glomerulus

options.label: B
options.text: The descending loop of Henle

options.label: C
options.text: The renal pyramid

options.label: D
options.text: The renal papilla

options.label: E
options.text: All of the above

questions.why: A renal corpuscle comprises the glomerular capillary tuft and the surrounding Bowman’s capsule. The capsule collects filtered fluid and delivers it to the proximal tubule at the urinary pole.

notes.B: The descending limb is a tubular segment that receives filtrate after it has passed through the proximal tubule.
notes.C: A renal pyramid is a medullary region containing straight tubules, ducts and vessels. The corpuscle is microscopic and cortical.
notes.D: The papilla is the tip of a renal pyramid where the collecting system discharges urine into a minor calyx.
notes.E: Only the capillary tuft and its surrounding capsule form the corpuscle. The loop, pyramid and papilla are separate structures.

questions.stem: Which of the following acts as the trigger for the initiation of micturition?

options.label: A
options.text: Stretching of the bladder wall

options.label: B
options.text: Motor neurons

options.label: C
options.text: The pressure of fluid in the bladder

options.label: D
options.text: Sympathetic efferents

options.label: E
options.text: A and B are correct

questions.why: Filling stretches the bladder wall and activates mechanosensitive afferents. Their signals reach sacral and higher centres, initiating the reflex that coordinates detrusor contraction and outlet relaxation.

notes.B: Motor output acts downstream of sensory signalling. It helps contract the detrusor and relax the external sphincter.
notes.C: Filling pressure relates to bladder distension, but the initiating sensory event is activation of wall stretch receptors.
notes.D: Sympathetic efferents mainly support urine storage. The voiding reflex begins with afferent signals from the bladder wall.
notes.E: Stretch supplies the initiating sensory signal. Motor neuron activity is part of the response after the signal reaches the cord.

questions.stem: The macula densa cells respond to

options.label: A
options.text: Aldosterone

options.label: B
options.text: Antidiuretic hormone

options.label: C
options.text: Changes in pressure in the tubule

options.label: D
options.text: Changes in solute content of the filtrate

options.label: E
options.text: Changes in the lining epithelium

questions.why: Macula densa cells detect changes in luminal sodium chloride at the end of the thick ascending limb. Their signals adjust afferent arteriolar tone and renin release.

notes.A: Aldosterone acts on cells of the distal nephron to regulate sodium reabsorption. The sensing role here concerns tubular sodium chloride.
notes.B: Vasopressin raises collecting duct water permeability. Macula densa cells monitor the sodium chloride content of tubular fluid.
notes.C: Pressure within the afferent arteriole can influence renin release through granular cells. The macula densa monitors luminal solute delivery.
notes.E: Macula densa cells are themselves specialised tubular epithelial cells. Their relevant stimulus is sodium chloride in the tubular lumen.

questions.stem: The fluid in the glomerular (Bowman's) capsule is similar to plasma EXCEPT that it does NOT contain a significant amount of

options.label: A
options.text: Glucose

options.label: B
options.text: Hormones

options.label: C
options.text: Electrolytes

options.label: D
options.text: Plasma proteins

options.label: E
options.text: Calcium ions

questions.why: Glomerular filtrate contains water and small dissolved solutes at concentrations close to the free plasma fractions. The filtration barrier holds back most plasma proteins, including most albumin.

notes.A: Glucose is small and freely filtered. It is normally reclaimed later by sodium-dependent transport in the proximal tubule.
notes.B: Small unbound hormones can pass through the filter. Protein binding or large molecular size limits filtration of other hormones.
notes.C: Small dissolved ions generally pass the glomerular filter. Tubular transport then adjusts their final urinary concentrations.
notes.E: The ionised and small complexed fractions of calcium can be filtered. Calcium bound to plasma protein is largely retained.

questions.stem: Alcohol acts as a diuretic because it

options.label: A
options.text: Is not reabsorbed by the tubule cells

options.label: B
options.text: Increases the rate of glomerular filtration

options.label: C
options.text: Increases secretion of ADH

options.label: D
options.text: Inhibits the release of ADH

options.label: E
options.text: Inhibits the release of ACTH

questions.why: Acute alcohol intake can suppress vasopressin release. Collecting ducts then reabsorb less water, so more dilute urine is passed while the reduction in vasopressin persists.

notes.A: The characteristic acute water diuresis is due to altered vasopressin release. It does not depend on alcohol remaining in the tubular lumen.
notes.B: An increase in filtration is not needed. Dilute urine results when less water is reabsorbed downstream in the collecting duct.
notes.C: Increased vasopressin would raise collecting duct water permeability. That favours water conservation rather than dilute urine.
notes.E: ACTH acts on the adrenal cortex. Collecting duct water permeability is controlled mainly by vasopressin in this response.

questions.stem: The urinary system does all of the following EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: Excretes excess albumin

options.label: B
options.text: Regulates blood volume

options.label: C
options.text: Helps stabilize blood pH

options.label: D
options.text: Eliminates organic waste products

options.label: E
options.text: Regulates plasma electrolyte concentrations

questions.why: The kidneys regulate volume, pH and electrolyte composition and eliminate metabolic wastes. Most albumin remains in plasma, and proximal tubular retrieval limits normal urinary albumin loss.

notes.B: Renal control of water and sodium excretion helps preserve circulating blood volume over time.
notes.C: The kidneys reclaim bicarbonate and excrete acid as ammonium and titratable acid, helping stabilise blood pH.
notes.D: Filtration and tubular secretion help remove organic wastes, including urea and creatinine, in urine.
notes.E: The kidneys can change reabsorption or secretion of ions such as sodium and potassium to regulate their plasma concentrations.

questions.stem: When the level of ADH (antidiuretic hormone) decreases,

options.label: A
options.text: More urine is produced

options.label: B
options.text: Less urine is produced

options.label: C
options.text: The osmolarity of the urine decreases

options.label: D
options.text: Both A and C

options.label: E
options.text: Both B and C

questions.why: A fall in vasopressin lowers water permeability in the collecting ducts. Less water is reabsorbed, increasing urine volume and decreasing urine osmolality when other factors are unchanged.

notes.A: Urine volume rises because less water leaves the collecting ducts. This is paired with a decrease in urine concentration.
notes.B: Lower water permeability leaves more water in the tubular lumen, so a fall in urine output is the opposite prediction.
notes.C: Urine osmolality falls as the remaining solutes are diluted. The volume of urine rises at the same time.
notes.E: The concentration change is in the right direction, but lower vasopressin increases urine volume rather than reducing it.

questions.stem: Molecules about the size of ____ or larger are normally not allowed through the filtration membrane.

options.label: A
options.text: Sodium ions

options.label: B
options.text: Glucose

options.label: C
options.text: Albumin

options.label: D
options.text: Amino acids

options.label: E
options.text: Urea

questions.why: The glomerular barrier readily passes water and small solutes while strongly restricting proteins around the size of albumin or larger. A small amount of albumin can still be filtered.

notes.A: Sodium ions are far smaller than albumin and pass into the filtrate. Their final excretion depends on tubular transport.
notes.B: Glucose is a small freely filtered solute and is normally reclaimed by proximal tubular cells.
notes.D: Free amino acids pass through the filter and are then substantially reabsorbed by the proximal tubule.
notes.E: Urea is a small freely filtered waste product and is also transported in parts of the tubule.

questions.stem: The process of filtration is driven by

options.label: A
options.text: Active transport

options.label: B
options.text: Blood osmotic pressure

options.label: C
options.text: Blood hydrostatic pressure

options.label: D
options.text: Renal pumping

options.label: E
options.text: Solvent drag

questions.why: Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure drives plasma water and small solutes into Bowman’s space. Plasma oncotic pressure and hydrostatic pressure in Bowman’s space oppose that movement.

notes.A: Glomerular filtration occurs by pressure-driven bulk flow. Active transport is important later for handling solutes along the tubule.
notes.B: Plasma proteins generate colloid osmotic pressure that draws water into capillaries, opposing outward filtration.
notes.D: The kidney has no separate pump that pushes fluid across the glomerular barrier. The driving pressure comes from the circulation.
notes.E: Solvent drag describes solute carried with moving water. The hydrostatic pressure gradient drives the water movement first.

questions.stem: The chief force pushing water and solutes out of the blood across the filtration membrane is

options.label: A
options.text: The size and shape of the podocytes

options.label: B
options.text: The thickness of the capillary endothelium

options.label: C
options.text: Glomerular hydrostatic (blood) pressure

options.label: D
options.text: The size of the pores in the basement membrane

options.label: E
options.text: Plasma colloid osmotic pressure

questions.why: Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure supplies the main outward force for filtration. Barrier structure governs permeability, and retained plasma proteins provide an inward oncotic force.

notes.A: Podocyte shape and slit diaphragms influence what crosses. The driving force is a pressure difference across the barrier.
notes.B: The thin fenestrated endothelium provides a permeable surface. It does not generate the outward filtration pressure.
notes.D: The basement membrane helps determine which solutes can cross. Hydrostatic pressure provides the force moving fluid through it.
notes.E: The colloid osmotic pressure generated by plasma proteins draws water toward the capillaries and opposes net outward filtration.

questions.stem: The filtration membrane includes all EXCEPT

options.label: A
options.text: Glomerular endothelium

options.label: B
options.text: Podocytes

options.label: C
options.text: Renal fascia

options.label: D
options.text: Basement membrane

options.label: E
options.text: Filtration slit membranes

questions.why: The glomerular filter consists of fenestrated capillary endothelium, a shared basement membrane and podocyte slit diaphragms. Renal fascia is a gross connective tissue sheath around the kidney.

notes.A: Fenestrated capillary endothelium forms the innermost layer that plasma encounters on the filtration path.
notes.B: Podocyte foot processes cover the abluminal side of the glomerular capillaries and form the final epithelial layer.
notes.D: The shared glomerular basement membrane lies between capillary endothelium and the podocyte foot processes.
notes.E: Slit diaphragms bridge the spaces between neighbouring podocyte foot processes and provide part of the filtration barrier.

questions.stem: Spermatogenesis is:

options.label: A
options.text: Achieved under the influence of testosterone

options.label: B
options.text: Possible to a certain degree even in old age

options.label: C
options.text: Dependent on Sertoli cell activity

notes.A: Leydig cells produce testosterone, which acts through androgen-responsive cells including Sertoli cells to support germ cell development.
notes.B: The seminiferous epithelium can remain active in older adults, although sperm output and quality may decline.
notes.C: Sertoli cells support developing germ cells, maintain their local environment and help coordinate maturation and release.

questions.why: Spermatogenesis requires high intratesticular testosterone and support from Sertoli cells inside seminiferous tubules. Production may continue into older age, although its efficiency can decline.

questions.stem: Sertoli cells:

options.label: A
options.text: Respond to Follicle Stimulating Hormone

options.label: B
options.text: Are contractile and produce androgen-binding protein

options.label: C
options.text: Are present in the testicular interstitium and perform a nurse function to the developing spermatocytes

options.label: D
options.text: Are phagocytic and very sensitive to high temperatures, malnutrition and X-rays

options.label: E
options.text: Are large irregular cells found in the tubuli recti and the seminiferous tubules

notes.A: Sertoli cells express follicle-stimulating hormone receptors and respond by supporting the environment required for spermatogenesis.
notes.B: Sertoli cells make androgen-binding protein. Contraction of the peritubular wall is a function of surrounding myoid cells.
notes.C: The nurse-cell function is correct, but Sertoli cells lie within the seminiferous epithelium. Leydig cells occupy the interstitium.
notes.D: Sertoli cells phagocytose residual bodies. Dividing germ cells are generally more vulnerable than Sertoli cells to heat and irradiation.
notes.E: Large irregular Sertoli cells are found in seminiferous tubules and form the lining at the beginning of the straight tubules.

questions.why: Sertoli cells support germ cells within seminiferous tubules, respond to follicle-stimulating hormone and secrete androgen-binding protein. They also help form the blood–testis barrier and clear residual bodies.

questions.stem: Myoid cells of the testis:

options.label: A
options.text: Contain actin microfilaments

options.label: B
options.text: Are present in the tunica albuginea and basal lamina of seminiferous tubules

options.label: C
options.text: Surround the seminiferous tubules

options.label: D
options.text: Are peritubular flattened cells of the seminiferous tubules

options.label: E
options.text: Aid movement of the male germ cells and testicular fluid

notes.A: Actin microfilaments support contraction and help give peritubular myoid cells their smooth-muscle-like properties.
notes.B: The characteristic peritubular cells lie outside the epithelial basal lamina, in the connective tissue coat surrounding each tubule.
notes.C: The myoid cells encircle the seminiferous tubules as part of the peritubular wall.
notes.D: They are flattened contractile cells arranged in layers of the tunica propria outside the seminiferous epithelium.
notes.E: Contraction of the peritubular wall helps move testicular fluid and newly released sperm that have limited motility.

questions.why: Peritubular myoid cells are flattened, actin-rich cells around seminiferous tubules. Their contraction helps propel testicular fluid and released germ cells toward the rete testis.

questions.stem: The efferent ductules:

options.label: A
options.text: Composed of alternating groups of tall ciliated columnar cells and short columnar cells with a brushborder

options.label: B
options.text: Lined by pseudostratified columnar with stereocilia

options.label: C
options.text: Surrounded by smooth muscle cells

options.label: D
options.text: Similar in structure to the ductus epididymis and vas deferens

options.label: E
options.text: For both motility and absorption

notes.A: Tall ciliated cells alternate with shorter cells bearing absorptive microvilli, giving sections a characteristic scalloped outline.
notes.B: Long stereocilia are prominent on epididymal principal cells. Efferent ductules have true motile cilia on some cells.
notes.C: A thin smooth muscle layer surrounds the ductules and aids transport through the lumen.
notes.D: Their alternating epithelial heights differ from those of the epididymis, and their muscle coat is thinner than the vas deferens.
notes.E: Cilia and smooth muscle aid movement, while shorter cells absorb much of the testicular fluid.

questions.why: Efferent ductules have a scalloped lumen formed by alternating tall ciliated and shorter absorptive epithelial cells. The ductules reclaim fluid and help transport sperm toward the epididymis.

questions.stem: The epididymis:

options.label: A
options.text: Has a tail that undergoes few peristaltic contractions because it serves as the principal reservoir for mature sperm

options.label: B
options.text: Is lined by pseudostratified columnar stereociliated epithelium with a smooth luminal margin

options.label: C
options.text: Is surrounded by smooth muscle cells

options.label: D
options.text: Is a site for spermatozoa storage and maturation, fluid absorption, phagocytosis of any residual bodies and degenerated sperms

options.label: E
options.text: Secretes glycerophosphocholine, sialic acid, and glycoproteins

notes.A: The tail acts as a reservoir with relatively little spontaneous movement during storage. Stronger contractions move sperm during ejaculation.
notes.B: Principal cells have stereocilia. The general epithelial outline is more even than the scalloped lining of efferent ductules.
notes.C: Smooth muscle encircles the duct and becomes thicker toward the tail, contributing to transport.
notes.D: The epididymis absorbs fluid, clears cellular debris and supports sperm maturation. Its tail stores mature sperm.
notes.E: The epithelium modifies epididymal fluid by adding compounds such as glycerophosphocholine and glycoproteins.

questions.why: The epididymal epithelium absorbs fluid and modifies luminal contents as sperm mature. Smooth muscle helps move sperm along the duct, and the tail serves as the main storage region.

questions.stem: The seminal vesicles:

options.label: A
options.text: Are a source of fructose that provides energy for spermatozoa, ascorbic acid, and prostaglandins

options.label: B
options.text: Are similar in structure to the ampulla of the ductus deferens and contain smooth muscle in their walls

options.label: C
options.text: Are sites of spermatozoa storage and maturation

options.label: D
options.text: Have a muscularis mucosae that contracts during ejaculation to discharge their secretion into the ejaculatory ducts and helps to flush sperm out of the urethra

notes.A: The secretions include fructose as an energy substrate for sperm, as well as prostaglandins and ascorbate.
notes.B: Both the seminal vesicle and terminal ampulla show a folded mucosa with a smooth muscle wall, though their glandular functions differ.
notes.C: Sperm mature and are stored mainly in the epididymis. The seminal vesicles provide fluid added during ejaculation.
notes.D: Secretions are expelled by smooth muscle in the gland wall, which is a muscular coat rather than a muscularis mucosae.

questions.why: Seminal vesicles are folded secretory glands that contribute fructose-rich fluid to semen. Smooth muscle in their walls contracts during ejaculation, delivering secretions into the ejaculatory ducts.

questions.stem: The prostate gland:

options.label: A
options.text: Similar in structure to the seminal vesicles but lacks smooth muscle in its wall

options.label: B
options.text: Posterior to the inferior border of the symphysis pubis and the pubic arch and serves as a site of spermatozoa storage and maturation

options.label: C
options.text: The largest accessory sex gland that secretes fibrinoysin, Acid phosphatase and citric acid

options.label: D
options.text: Has acidophilic smooth muscle cells between the secretory alveoli and acidophilic concretions within the alveoli

notes.A: The prostate has abundant smooth muscle between its glands as part of its fibromuscular stroma.
notes.B: The prostate lies behind the pubic symphysis, but sperm mature and are stored in the epididymis.
notes.C: Prostatic secretion contains citrate, acid phosphatase and enzymes that break down the seminal coagulum after ejaculation.
notes.D: Eosinophilic smooth muscle lies between secretory glands. Rounded prostatic concretions may be seen within glandular lumina.

questions.why: The prostate is the largest male accessory gland. Its tubuloalveolar glands sit in fibromuscular stroma and secrete citrate, acid phosphatase and proteases that help liquefy semen.

questions.stem: After vasectomy:

options.label: A
options.text: Penile erection is possible

options.label: B
options.text: Normal sexual relations are impaired

options.label: C
options.text: Spermatozoa may be found in the ejaculate for 60 days or more

options.label: D
options.text: Production of spermatozoa continue to old age

options.label: E
options.text: Fertility is impaired

notes.A: Erection depends on neurovascular pathways and erectile tissue. These are separate from the interrupted sperm ducts.
notes.B: Libido, erection and ejaculation generally remain possible. Most ejaculate volume comes from accessory gland secretions.
notes.C: Residual sperm can persist for weeks or months, which is why post-vasectomy semen testing is used to confirm clearance.
notes.D: Testicular spermatogenesis can continue after the ducts are interrupted, including into older age.
notes.E: The procedure is intended to prevent sperm from reaching the ejaculate once post-vasectomy semen clearance is confirmed.

questions.why: Vasectomy interrupts sperm transport through the ductus deferens while preserving testosterone production and erectile function. Sperm already beyond the interruption can remain in ejaculates until cleared.

questions.stem: The ejaculatory duct:

options.label: A
options.text: It has no muscle in its wall; the fibromuscular tissue of the prostate substitutes for its muscularis

options.label: B
options.text: Its muscular coat consists of two layer

options.label: C
options.text: It is lined by pseudostratified columnar epithelium

options.label: D
options.text: It conducts sperm

options.label: E
options.text: It contains sertoli cells

notes.A: The intraprostatic passage lacks a distinct muscular coat of its own and lies within fibromuscular prostatic tissue.
notes.B: A layered muscular coat is characteristic of the ductus deferens. The ejaculatory duct lacks a separate two-layer muscle coat.
notes.C: Pseudostratified columnar epithelium can line the ejaculatory duct, with variation along the passage.
notes.D: Sperm arrive from the ductus deferens and pass through the ejaculatory duct with fluid from the seminal vesicle.
notes.E: Sertoli cells support germ cells in the seminiferous epithelium. They are absent from the ejaculatory duct lining.

questions.why: The ductus deferens and seminal vesicle duct unite to form each ejaculatory duct. The duct traverses the prostate to deliver sperm and seminal vesicle fluid into the urethra.

questions.stem: The glans penis:

options.label: A
options.text: Projects backwards and laterally to cover the distal ends of the corpora cavernosa

options.label: B
options.text: Contains the fossa navicularis of the urethra that is lined with stratified columnar epithelium

options.label: C
options.text: Consists only of convolutions of large veins, and it does not reach the same state of rigidity as the shaft of the erect penis

options.label: D
options.text: Consists of the urethra, three cavernous bodies and a prepuce that resembles a mucous membrane on its inner aspect

notes.A: It caps the distal ends of the corpora cavernosa.
notes.B: Non-keratinized stratified squamous.
notes.C: Its erectile tissue is convoluted veins, so it never becomes as rigid as the shaft.
notes.D: The glans contains only the corpus spongiosum, not three cavernous bodies.

questions.why: The glans is the expanded end of the corpus spongiosum, made of large convoluted veins, so it stays softer than the shaft; the fossa navicularis is lined by stratified squamous epithelium.

questions.stem: About testicular function:

options.label: A
options.text: The cooler venous blood returning from the testis and scrotum cools the arterial blood before it enters the testis

options.label: B
options.text: Dividing populations of germ cells are very sensitive to radiation

options.label: C
options.text: Prolonged residence of the testis within the abdomen results in progressive degeneration of germ cells

options.label: D
options.text: Frequent immersions in hot baths or wearing close-fitting, tight trousers may result in fewer sperm in the ejaculate

notes.A: The pampiniform venous plexus carries relatively cooler blood around branches of the testicular artery, allowing heat exchange before arterial entry.
notes.B: Proliferating germ cells, especially dividing spermatogonia, are vulnerable to ionising radiation because DNA damage can interrupt cell division.
notes.C: An undescended abdominal testis remains at a higher temperature than a scrotal testis, which can impair the germinal epithelium over time.
notes.D: Repeated hot-water exposure can impair semen measures. Studies of tight clothing are less consistent, so this is a possible association.

questions.why: Spermatogenesis is temperature-sensitive. Countercurrent heat exchange in the spermatic cord helps cool incoming arterial blood, and sustained increases in testicular temperature can impair germ cell development.

questions.stem: The interstitial tissue of the testis contains:

options.label: A
options.text: A rich blood supply

options.label: B
options.text: An extensive network of lymphatic vessels

options.label: C
options.text: Fenestrated capillaries

options.label: D
options.text: Leydig cells and Call Exner bodies

options.label: E
options.text: Leydig cells and Sertoli cells

notes.A: It has a rich blood supply for hormone transport.
notes.B: It has an extensive lymphatic network.
notes.C: Fenestrated capillaries carry testosterone away from the Leydig cells.
notes.D: Call-Exner bodies are in ovarian follicles.
notes.E: Sertoli cells are inside the tubules.

questions.why: The testicular interstitium has Leydig cells among blood vessels, fenestrated capillaries and many lymphatics; Sertoli cells are inside the tubules and Call-Exner bodies are ovarian.

questions.stem: The vulva:

options.label: A
options.text: Consists of the mons pubis, labia majora, labia minora, vestibule of the vagina, vestibular glands and the clitoris

options.label: B
options.text: The labia minora are two elongated hairless folds that enclose the pudendal/urogenital cleft

options.label: C
options.text: The labia majora are two small hairless folds of skin located between the labia majora at either side of the opening of the vagina

options.label: D
options.text: The clitoris consists of erectile tissue that is richly innervated with sensory endings and is capable of enlargement as a result of engorgement with blood

options.label: E
options.text: The clitoris is traversed by the urethra

notes.A: These are the parts of the vulva.
notes.B: The labia majora enclose the cleft.
notes.C: That describes the labia minora.
notes.D: The clitoris is richly innervated erectile tissue that engorges with blood.
notes.E: It is not.

questions.why: The vulva is the mons, labia majora (hairy, enclosing the cleft), labia minora (hairless), vestibule, vestibular glands and clitoris; the urethra opens in the vestibule, not through the clitoris.

questions.stem: The cervical mucosa (endocervix):

options.label: A
options.text: Lacks spiral arteries and contains large branched tubular glands

options.label: B
options.text: Undergoes very little change in thickness during the menstrual cycle and is not sloughed off during menstruation

options.label: C
options.text: Secretes a fluid that is voluminous and thin in consistency at ovulation and can be penetrated by spermatozoa more readily

options.label: D
options.text: Secretes a thick mucoid product that acts as a barrier to sperm transport in the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle

options.label: E
options.text: Blockage of the openings of the cervical glands results in the retention of their secretions and formation of dilated cysts known as Nabothian cysts

notes.A: The endocervix has deep branching mucus-secreting glands. Spiral arteries are characteristic of the functional endometrium of the uterine body.
notes.B: Endocervical secretion changes with the cycle, but its lining does not undergo menstrual shedding like the endometrial functional layer.
notes.C: Around ovulation, oestrogen promotes more abundant, less viscous mucus that sperm can traverse more readily.
notes.D: Progesterone favours thicker cervical mucus after ovulation, reducing receptivity to sperm passage.
notes.E: A blocked cervical gland opening can trap mucus and distend the gland, forming a Nabothian cyst.

questions.why: Endocervical glands remain intact during menstruation and change their mucus under hormonal influence. Mucus is thinner around ovulation, while obstruction of a gland opening can produce a retention cyst.

questions.stem: Uterine and ovarian changes in pregnancy:

options.label: A
options.text: The smooth muscle cells of the uterus increase greatly in length during pregnancy from 50µm to 500µm

options.label: B
options.text: There is a striking growth of the blood vessels

options.label: C
options.text: The corpus luteum persists to produce progesterone

options.label: D
options.text: The corpus luteum regresses and both progesterone and oestrogen production ceases

notes.A: Myometrial smooth muscle cells enlarge markedly in pregnancy. The stated lengths illustrate the approximate scale of hypertrophy.
notes.B: Uterine vascular growth and remodelling support the increased demands of the uterus and developing placenta.
notes.C: Early trophoblastic human chorionic gonadotrophin maintains the corpus luteum and its progesterone output until the placenta takes over.
notes.D: The corpus luteum can regress after the luteal–placental shift, but placental production of progesterone and oestrogens continues.

questions.why: The growing uterus develops longer, larger myometrial cells and a greatly expanded blood supply. Early in pregnancy the corpus luteum supplies progesterone before the placenta assumes most production.

questions.stem: Lactation and fertility:

options.label: A
options.text: Lactational amenorrhoea is due to high levels of serum Prolactin

options.label: B
options.text: High serum Prolactin suppresses secretion of Luteinizing hormone

options.label: C
options.text: Resumption of ovulation occurs with a decrease in suckling frequency

options.label: D
options.text: Lactational amenorrhoea is a means of birth control

notes.A: Frequent suckling sustains prolactin release and contributes to the suppression of the reproductive axis during lactation.
notes.B: Elevated prolactin contributes to reduced pulsatile gonadotrophin-releasing hormone signalling and hence reduced luteinising hormone pulsatility.
notes.C: When suckling becomes less frequent, reproductive hormonal signalling can recover and ovulation may resume before the first bleed.
notes.D: The lactational amenorrhoea method requires absent menses, full or nearly full breastfeeding, and an infant younger than six months.

questions.why: Frequent suckling raises prolactin and suppresses hypothalamic reproductive signalling. Reduced pulsatile luteinising hormone delays ovulation, and ovarian cycles can resume as suckling becomes less frequent.

questions.stem: The coiled (spiral) arteries of the endometrium:

options.label: A
options.text: Are present in the uterine cervix

options.label: B
options.text: Constrict and close off blood supply at the end of the secretory phase

options.label: C
options.text: Are found in the stratum functionalis

options.label: D
options.text: Develop again during each menstrual cycle

options.label: E
options.text: Are well developed during the mid-secretory phase

notes.A: Spiral arteries serve the endometrium of the uterine body. The mucus-secreting endocervix does not have this cyclic arterial arrangement.
notes.B: Loss of luteal progesterone is associated with intermittent constriction of spiral arteries and breakdown of the functional layer.
notes.C: Spiral arteries rise from the basal region and supply the overlying stratum functionalis, which is shed during menstruation.
notes.D: After menstruation the functional layer regrows and its spiral arteries lengthen again from vessels retained in the basal layer.
notes.E: The vessels elongate and coil as the endometrium develops, becoming well developed in the secretory phase.

questions.why: Spiral arteries supply the endometrial functional layer and lengthen as it regenerates. After progesterone withdrawal, late-cycle vasoconstriction contributes to breakdown of this layer during menstruation.

questions.stem: The cervical wall:

options.label: A
options.text: Contains a limited number of smooth muscle cells (15%) and a large amount of dense connective tissue

options.label: B
options.text: Has a complex pattern of connective tissue and smooth muscle

options.label: C
options.text: Regulates access to the uterine cavity and dilates for the emergence of the newborn

options.label: D
options.text: Consists largely of collagenous fibers, some elastic fibers along the outermost surface and relatively little smooth muscle

notes.A: The cervix has much less smooth muscle than the uterine body. A figure near fifteen percent is approximate and varies by region.
notes.B: Collagen-rich connective tissue, elastic fibres and smooth muscle are distributed unevenly through the cervical wall.
notes.C: The cervix controls access to the uterine cavity, then softens and dilates to allow passage of the fetus during labour.
notes.D: Collagen is the dominant component. Elastic fibres and a smaller smooth muscle component contribute to cervical mechanical properties.

questions.why: Dense collagen-rich connective tissue makes up much of the cervical wall. Its matrix helps the cervix remain closed during pregnancy and remodel to permit dilatation during labour.

questions.stem: All of the following about granulosa lutein cells are true EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: They are the predominant cell type in the corpus luteum

options.label: B
options.text: They are derived from the theca interna

options.label: C
options.text: They contain abundant smooth endoplasmic reticulum

options.label: D
options.text: They are large and pale-staining

options.label: E
options.text: They secrete progesterone

questions.why: Granulosa lutein cells form when follicular granulosa cells luteinise after ovulation. These large, pale steroid-producing cells differ from the smaller theca lutein cells derived from theca interna.

notes.A: Granulosa lutein cells make up much of the corpus luteum and are prominent in routine histological sections.
notes.C: Abundant smooth endoplasmic reticulum is typical of steroid-producing cells and contributes to progesterone synthesis.
notes.D: Granulosa lutein cells are large and relatively pale, in part because their steroidogenic cytoplasm contains lipid droplets.
notes.E: Progesterone secreted by the corpus luteum acts on endometrial glands and stroma to maintain the secretory state.

questions.stem: Decidual cells:

options.label: A
options.text: Differentiate from endometrial epithelium

options.label: B
options.text: Secrete prolactin

options.label: C
options.text: Control the invasion of the trophoblast and acts as an immunological barrier that protects the embryo from maternal immune rejection

notes.A: Decidual cells arise from stromal fibroblast-like cells below the epithelium. They enlarge and change their secretory activity.
notes.B: Decidual prolactin is produced locally and is commonly used as a marker of endometrial stromal decidualisation.
notes.C: Decidual cells help regulate trophoblast depth and contribute to the local immune environment that supports implantation.

questions.why: Decidual cells develop from progesterone-responsive endometrial stromal cells. They release factors including prolactin and help regulate trophoblast invasion and maternal immune adaptation at the implantation site.

questions.stem: Corpora lutea:

options.label: A
options.text: Develop after ovulation from the theca folliculi only

options.label: B
options.text: Possess both granulosa lutein cells and theca lutein cells

options.label: C
options.text: Develop under the influence of Luteininizing hormone and are yellow in appearance

options.label: D
options.text: Have lipid-rich cells and secrete both oestrogen and progesterone

notes.A: The corpus luteum develops from both granulosa cells and cells of the theca interna in the ruptured follicle.
notes.B: Granulosa lutein cells are generally larger and paler, while theca lutein cells are smaller and lie near connective tissue septa.
notes.C: Luteinising hormone promotes luteinisation after ovulation. Lipid-associated pigment contributes to the yellow appearance.
notes.D: Both lutein cell populations contain lipid and participate in steroid production. The corpus luteum secretes progesterone and oestrogens.

questions.why: The luteinising hormone surge promotes luteinisation after ovulation. Granulosa and theca interna cells form distinct steroid-producing populations within the yellow, lipid-rich corpus luteum.

questions.stem: Ovarian follicular atresia:

options.label: A
options.text: May occur at any stage of follicular development

options.label: B
options.text: Is characterized by disorganization of the granulosa cells

options.label: C
options.text: Is characterized by thickening of the basement membrane between the granulosa cells and theca Interna, known as the glassy membrane

options.label: D
options.text: Is characterized by disintegration of the oocyte and persistence of the collapsed zona pellucida

options.label: E
options.text: May involve invasion of the follicle by connective tissue

notes.A: Atresia can occur at several stages, from early growing follicles to large antral follicles.
notes.B: Granulosa cells undergo apoptosis and lose their regular arrangement, particularly in atretic antral follicles.
notes.C: Thickening of the basement membrane between the granulosa and theca can produce the characteristic glassy membrane.
notes.D: The oocyte can disintegrate while its surrounding zona pellucida persists transiently as a collapsed remnant.
notes.E: Connective tissue may enter the degenerating follicle and replace its former cellular and fluid spaces.

questions.why: Follicular atresia is degeneration rather than ovulation and can affect follicles at different developmental stages. In larger follicles, granulosa cells, the oocyte and the follicular basement membrane show characteristic changes.

questions.stem: Variations in the wall of the uterine tube:

options.label: A
options.text: Mucosal folds reach their greatest height and complexity in the ampulla and are reduced in both Size and complexity closer to the uterus

options.label: B
options.text: Ciliated cells are usually more numerous at the infundibular end of uterine tube whereas secretory cells tend to predominate at the uterine end

options.label: C
options.text: The number of ciliated cells increase from the infundibulum to the interstitial segment whereas the number of secretory cells decrease from the infundibulum to the interstitial segment

options.label: D
options.text: Ciliated cells are more numerous during the follicular phase of the cycle, whereas secretory cells predominate during the luteal phase

options.label: E
options.text: Ciliation is progesterone-dependent

notes.A: Tall, branching mucosal folds nearly fill the ampullary lumen. The isthmus and intramural segment have simpler folds.
notes.B: Ciliated epithelial cells are generally more prominent near the infundibulum, with more secretory cells toward the uterine end.
notes.C: The expected regional tendency is reversed here. Distal segments are usually more densely ciliated than proximal segments.
notes.D: Oestrogen during the follicular phase favours ciliation, while secretory activity becomes more prominent during the luteal phase.
notes.E: Oestrogen favours ciliogenesis. Progesterone has a greater role in luteal-phase secretory changes and can reduce ciliary activity.

questions.why: Uterine tube folds are most complex in the ampulla and decrease toward the uterus. Ciliated cells favour the distal region and oestrogen-dominant phase, while secretory cells are more prominent proximally.

questions.stem: The uterus:

options.label: A
options.text: Has a functionalis which is shed at menses

options.label: B
options.text: Has a basalis that lacks glands and is adjacent to the myometrium and is retained at menstruation

options.label: C
options.text: Has a fundus that is the usual site of implantation

notes.A: The functional portion undergoes cyclic changes and is the layer lost during menstrual shedding.
notes.B: The basal layer remains against the myometrium and retains the deep portions of endometrial glands, which help regenerate the lining.
notes.C: Normal implantation favours the upper uterine cavity, often along an anterior or posterior wall in the fundal region.

questions.why: The superficial functional endometrium is shed at menstruation and regrows from retained basal tissue. Implantation usually occurs high in the uterine cavity near the fundus.

questions.stem: The thyroid gland:

options.label: A
options.text: Has follicles that are roughly spheroid cyst-like compartments with walls formed by a simple squamous or cuboidal epithelium

options.label: B
options.text: Has follicles that are filled with a gel-like mass that contains thyroglobulin, the inactive storage form of the thyroid hormones

options.label: C
options.text: Has parafollicular cells within the follicular epithelium or scattered in the interfollicular connective tissue

options.label: D
options.text: Parafollicular cells secrete a hormone that reduces the level of calcium in the blood

options.label: E
options.text: Thyroid hormones are essential for fetal development and regulate metabolism

notes.A: Follicles are approximately spherical. Their simple lining is often cuboidal and can flatten when relatively inactive.
notes.B: Colloid contains thyroglobulin with iodinated residues from which active thyroid hormones are released after uptake and processing.
notes.C: Parafollicular cells occur at the base of follicular epithelium or between follicles and generally do not reach the colloid.
notes.D: Calcitonin from parafollicular cells can lower blood calcium in part by reducing osteoclast-mediated bone resorption.
notes.E: Thyroid hormones are important for fetal growth and nervous system development and help regulate energy expenditure after birth.

questions.why: Thyroid follicular cells produce iodinated thyroglobulin and store it in luminal colloid. Parafollicular cells secrete calcitonin, while follicular thyroid hormones support development and regulate metabolic activity.

questions.stem: The parathyroid glands:

options.label: A
options.text: Are usually found embedded in the thyroid gland and function in the regulation of blood ion levels of calcium and phosphate

options.label: B
options.text: Have more numerous principal/chief cells with pale-staining, slightly acidophilic cytoplasm, centrally located nuclei and large accumulations of glycogen and lipid droplets

options.label: C
options.text: Have oxyphil cells that are larger than chief cells

notes.A: The calcium and phosphate function is correct. The glands are usually on the posterior surface rather than embedded within thyroid parenchyma.
notes.B: Chief cells predominate and have central nuclei and relatively pale cytoplasm. Glycogen and lipid content varies with cell state.
notes.C: Oxyphil cells are larger and contain many mitochondria, which give the cytoplasm its strong eosinophilia.

questions.why: The parathyroids usually lie along the posterior thyroid surface. Chief cells secrete parathyroid hormone to regulate calcium and phosphate, while oxyphil cells are larger and more intensely eosinophilic.

questions.stem: The islets of Langerhans:

options.label: A
options.text: Contain Alpha and Beta cells

options.label: B
options.text: The alpha cells secrete insulin and the Beta cells secrete glucagon

options.label: C
options.text: Contain ducts for transport of its secretory products and rosette-shaped secretory acini

options.label: D
options.text: Are richly vascularised for transport of its secretory products

options.label: E
options.text: Secrete somatostatin

notes.A: Alpha and beta cells are two major populations among the endocrine cells of the islets.
notes.B: Beta cells release insulin to reduce blood glucose, while alpha cells release glucagon to increase it.
notes.C: Acini and ducts belong to the exocrine pancreas. Islet products enter the local capillary network.
notes.D: A rich network of capillaries provides a route for islet hormones to enter the circulation.
notes.E: Delta cells secrete somatostatin, which helps regulate hormone secretion within the islet.

questions.why: Pancreatic islets are ductless endocrine cell clusters closely associated with capillaries. Beta cells release insulin, alpha cells release glucagon and delta cells secrete somatostatin.

questions.stem: The adrenal gland:

options.label: A
options.text: Is organized into cortical protein-secreting and medullary, catecholamine-secreting portions

options.label: B
options.text: The cortex is the steroid-secreting portion and constitutes nearly 90% of the weight of the gland

options.label: C
options.text: The medulla is divided into Zona glomerulosa, Zona fasciculata, and Zona reticualris,

options.label: D
options.text: The cells of the zona glomerulosa are arranged in closely packed ovoid clusters whereas the cells of zona fasciculata are arranged in long straight cords separated by the sinusoidal capillaries

notes.A: The medulla secretes catecholamines. The cortex produces steroids derived from cholesterol, rather than protein hormones.
notes.B: The cortex constitutes roughly nine-tenths of the gland and supplies mineralocorticoids, glucocorticoids and androgens.
notes.C: The three named zones are cortical layers. The medulla lies centrally and has chromaffin cells.
notes.D: Glomerulosa cells form small rounded groups, while fasciculata cells form radial cords separated by sinusoidal capillaries.

questions.why: The adrenal cortex accounts for most of the gland and synthesises steroid hormones in three zones. The medulla contains chromaffin cells that release catecholamines.

questions.stem: Junctional complexes are located on the:

options.label: A
options.text: Apical membrane only

options.label: B
options.text: Basal and lateral membranes only

options.label: C
options.text: Lateral membrane only

options.label: D
options.text: Apical and basal membranes

notes.A: The apical membrane faces the lumen. The complex lies just below it at the lateral boundary between adjacent cells.
notes.B: The complex is lateral near the apex. Basal attachments such as hemidesmosomes connect cells to extracellular matrix.
notes.C: The lateral membranes of neighbouring cells meet at the apicolateral complex, which seals and mechanically links them.
notes.D: The basal membrane contacts the basal lamina. The junctional complex joins cell to cell at the apicolateral border.

questions.why: The classical epithelial junctional complex is arranged along the apicolateral membrane where neighbouring cells meet. It includes tight junctions, adherens junctions and desmosomes in sequence.

questions.stem: An epithelium has both microvilli and cilia. It:

options.label: A
options.text: Was normally subjected to severe mechanical stresses

options.label: B
options.text: Is from a surface where both absorption and motility are required

options.label: C
options.text: Is from a chamber that changes its volume continually

notes.A: Stratified squamous epithelium is a common adaptation to mechanical abrasion. Microvilli and cilia suggest transport-related roles.
notes.B: Microvilli enlarge the absorptive surface and beating cilia move luminal contents along or mix the local fluid.
notes.C: Urothelium adapts to substantial changes in volume through superficial cells that flatten during distension.

questions.why: Microvilli increase apical surface area for exchange, whereas motile cilia move luminal contents. Efferent ductules illustrate this combination through adjacent absorptive and ciliated cell populations.

questions.stem: The lateral border between two epithelial cells carries:

options.label: A
options.text: Hemidesmosomes and desmosomes

options.label: B
options.text: Tight junctions, adhering junctions and hemidesmosomes

options.label: C
options.text: Cilia, desmosomes and zona occludens

options.label: D
options.text: Zonula occludens and zonula adherens only

options.label: E
options.text: Zonula adherens and macula adherens only

notes.A: Desmosomes can join adjacent cells laterally. Hemidesmosomes attach the basal cell surface to the basal lamina.
notes.B: Tight and adherens junctions are lateral, but hemidesmosomes anchor the basal surface to extracellular matrix.
notes.C: Desmosomes and tight junctions are lateral. Cilia project from the free apical surface into the lumen.
notes.D: Both junctions are present, but desmosomes and gap junctions can also lie on lateral membranes.
notes.E: Both adhesion junctions are lateral, but tight junctions and gap junctions can also occupy this border.

questions.why: Epithelial lateral membranes carry several cell-to-cell junctions. Near the apex, tight and adherens junctions are followed by desmosomes, while gap junctions can occur elsewhere laterally.

questions.stem: Epithelial cells specialized for ion transport are found in the:

options.label: A
options.text: Skin

options.label: B
options.text: Ducts of salivary glands

options.label: C
options.text: Ducts of pancreas

options.label: D
options.text: Kidney tubules

options.label: E
options.text: Choroid plexus

notes.A: Surface epidermis is mainly a keratinised protective barrier. Ion-transporting ducts associated with skin are distinct epithelial structures.
notes.B: Striated salivary ducts modify the primary secretion by transporting ions, including reabsorbing sodium and secreting potassium.
notes.C: Pancreatic duct cells secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid, which carries enzymes and helps neutralise acid in the duodenum.
notes.D: Renal tubular epithelia selectively reabsorb and secrete ions to regulate body fluid composition.
notes.E: The choroid plexus epithelium transports ions to drive water movement into cerebrospinal fluid.

questions.why: Ion-transporting epithelia use channels, pumps and transporters to alter fluid composition. Salivary and pancreatic ducts, renal tubules and choroid plexus are specialised examples in different organs.

questions.stem: About epithelial tissues:

options.label: A
options.text: Junctional complexes are found at numerous sites between epithelial cells and their underlying connective tissue

options.label: B
options.text: Stereocilia are extremely long form of microvilli

options.label: C
options.text: The principal function of microvilli is to increase the surface area of cells

options.label: D
options.text: Desmosomes are sites of strong intercellular adhesion and provide points of attachment for elements of the cytoskeleton

options.label: E
options.text: Cilia constitute the characteristic brush border of the small intestine

notes.A: Classical junctional complexes connect adjacent epithelial cells. Cell-to-matrix contacts such as hemidesmosomes occur at the basal surface.
notes.B: Stereocilia are long, actin-based microvilli, such as those found on epididymal principal cells.
notes.C: Microvilli increase the apical membrane area available for absorption, secretion or interaction with the lumen.
notes.D: Desmosomes provide strong cell-to-cell adhesion by linking cytoskeletal intermediate filaments across adjacent cells.
notes.E: The intestinal brush border consists of tightly packed actin-based microvilli rather than motile cilia.

questions.why: Epithelial surface specialisations serve distinct functions. Microvilli expand membrane area, stereocilia are elongated microvilli, and desmosomes couple neighbouring cells through their intermediate filament networks.

questions.stem: An epithelium with a striated border:

options.label: A
options.text: It has tightly packed cilia and lines the respiratory tract

options.label: B
options.text: It has tightly packed microvilli and lines the uterus

options.label: C
options.text: It has tightly packed stereocilia and lines proximal segment of the nephron

options.label: D
options.text: It has tightly packed microtubules and lines floating chorionic villi

options.label: E
options.text: It has tightly packed microvilli and covers intestinal absorptive cells

notes.A: Respiratory cilia are longer, motile projections with microtubules. They move mucus rather than forming an absorptive striated border.
notes.B: Uterine epithelium can have ciliated and secretory cells, but the classical striated border identifies intestinal absorptive epithelium.
notes.C: The proximal renal tubule has a brush border of microvilli. Stereocilia are prominent in the epididymis.
notes.D: Syncytiotrophoblast on chorionic villi has surface microvilli, which have actin cores rather than microtubular axonemes.
notes.E: Uniform microvilli cover the apical surfaces of intestinal enterocytes and collectively form the striated border.

questions.why: The intestinal striated border is formed by densely packed, uniform microvilli on enterocytes. These apical projections increase absorptive surface area and contain bundles of actin.

questions.stem: A junctional complex includes:

options.label: A
options.text: A tight junction, a desmosome and a zonula adherens

options.label: B
options.text: A zonula adherens, a desmosome and a zonula occludens

options.label: C
options.text: A gap junction, a hemidesmosome and a tight junction

options.label: D
options.text: A tight junction, a basal lamina and a terminal web

options.label: E
options.text: A basal lamina, a hemidesmosome and a gap junction

notes.A: The tight junction seals the apex, the adherens belt anchors actin and the desmosome anchors intermediate filaments.
notes.B: Zonula occludens is the tight junction. Together with the zonula adherens and desmosome it completes the classical complex.
notes.C: Gap junctions allow communication, while hemidesmosomes anchor to basal matrix. They are outside the classical three-part complex.
notes.D: The basal lamina is extracellular and the terminal web is cytoplasmic. Neither is a cell-to-cell junction.
notes.E: The basal lamina and hemidesmosomes belong to the basal cell–matrix interface. A gap junction serves lateral communication.

questions.why: The classical junctional complex contains a tight junction, an adherens belt and a desmosome. These lateral contacts provide selective sealing and mechanical adhesion between neighbouring epithelial cells.

questions.stem: Goblet cells are found in the lining of:

options.label: A
options.text: Stomach and gallbladder

options.label: B
options.text: Ileum, colon, trachea and respiratory bronchioles

options.label: C
options.text: Large intestine, primary bronchi and gallbladder

options.label: D
options.text: Trachea, stomach, uterus, appendix

options.label: E
options.text: Jejunum, appendix and primary bronchi

notes.A: The stomach has surface mucous cells, while the normal gallbladder has absorptive columnar epithelium. Neither normally has goblet cells.
notes.B: Ileum, colon and trachea have goblet cells. Respiratory bronchioles have club cells and cuboidal lining cells between alveoli.
notes.C: Large intestine and primary bronchi have goblet cells. The normal gallbladder lining has absorptive columnar cells.
notes.D: The trachea and appendix contain goblet cells. Gastric surface mucous cells and uterine secretory cells are distinct cell types.
