notes.E: Jejunal and appendiceal epithelia contain goblet cells, as does the respiratory epithelium of the primary bronchi.

questions.why: Goblet cells secrete mucins in intestinal lining and in larger conducting airways. Normal gastric and gallbladder epithelia lack them, and respiratory bronchioles primarily have cuboidal and alveolar lining cells.

questions.stem: An Anatomy Professor examined three different specimens from unknown locations. He concluded that specimen A was taken from a chamber that changes its volume continually, specimen B was from a surface where both absorption and secretion are required and specimen C was from an internal surface where friction may occur. Specimens A, B, C were:

options.label: A
options.text: Transitional epithelium, simple columnar epithelium with goblets and a brushborder, stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium respectively

options.label: B
options.text: Simple columnar epithelium, simple columnar epithelium with goblets and a brushborder and stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium respectively

options.label: C
options.text: Transitional epithelium, stratified cuboidal and stratified squamous non-keratinized Epithelium respectively

options.label: D
options.text: Transitional epithelium, pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium with a brushborder, stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium respectively

options.label: E
options.text: Urinary bladder, small intestine and oesophagus respectively

notes.A: Urothelium stretches, intestinal enterocytes and goblet cells support absorption and secretion, and stratified squamous lining resists friction.
notes.B: Simple columnar epithelium fits the intestinal sample. Urothelium better fits a reservoir with repeated volume changes.
notes.C: Stratified cuboidal epithelium is typical of some ducts. Intestinal absorption and mucus secretion fit a columnar lining with goblet cells.
notes.D: Pseudostratified ciliated epithelium typically moves material along a surface. The absorbing and secreting sample fits intestinal epithelium.
notes.E: The bladder, small intestine and oesophagus are examples of the three environments, in the order specified in the question.

questions.why: Urothelium accommodates bladder distension, intestinal columnar epithelium absorbs and secretes, and non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium protects the oesophagus from abrasion on a moist surface.

questions.stem: A male Anatomy Professor also examined three different specimens from unknown locations. He concluded that specimen D was taken from a surface that was normally subjected to severe mechanical stresses, specimen E was from a surface where either filtration or diffusion occurs and specimen F was from an internal chamber where absorption and motility are required. Specimens D, E, F were obtained from:

options.label: A
options.text: Filiform papillae of tongue, parietal layer of renal corpuscle and epididymis respectively

options.label: B
options.text: Surfaces with stratified squamous keratinized epithelium, simple squamous epithelium and pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium with a brushborder respectively

options.label: C
options.text: Surfaces with stratified squamous keratinized epithelium, pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium with a brushborder and simple squamous epithelium respectively

notes.A: Filiform papillae resist friction, but the parietal capsule lies outside the filtration barrier and epididymal stereocilia are non-motile microvilli.
notes.B: The three linings match abrasion resistance, a short diffusion path and an epithelial surface combining microvillar absorption with ciliary movement.
notes.C: This places a ciliated transporting epithelium at the thin exchange surface and simple squamous epithelium at the absorptive motile surface.

questions.why: Keratinised stratified squamous epithelium resists severe surface stress, simple squamous epithelium provides a thin barrier, and epithelial microvilli and cilia can support absorption and luminal movement.

questions.stem: Transitional epithelium stops urine leaking between its cells through its:

options.label: A
options.text: Gap junctions

options.label: B
options.text: Tight junctions

options.label: C
options.text: Desmosomes

options.label: D
options.text: Terminal web

options.label: E
options.text: Hemidesmosomes

notes.A: Gap junctions allow ions and small molecules to pass directly between cells. They do not seal the extracellular pathway.
notes.B: Tight junctions restrict solute and water passage between adjacent umbrella cells near their apical borders.
notes.C: Desmosomes support mechanical adhesion between cells, while tight junctions provide the principal paracellular seal.
notes.D: The terminal web is a cytoskeletal network beneath an apical surface rather than an intercellular seal.
notes.E: Hemidesmosomes anchor epithelial cells to basal matrix. They do not join adjacent umbrella cells at the luminal border.

questions.why: Tight junctions between surface umbrella cells seal the paracellular route in urothelium. Their apical membrane specialisations also restrict movement of urine through the cells themselves.

questions.stem: You are given a specimen with several clusters of epithelial cells embedded completely in connective tissue. Some of the cell clusters were dark-stained with central round nuclei whereas others were pale-stained with peripheral flattened nuclei. In addition epithelially-lined passages that link the cell clusters to an epithelial-lined surface were present. The passages are unbranched. You identified the specimen

options.label: A
options.text: As simple squamous and simple cuboidal

options.label: B
options.text: As a simple endocrine gland with serous and mucous secretory units

options.label: C
options.text: As a simple exocrine gland with serous and mucous secretory units

options.label: D
options.text: Is from an organ which secretes a product

options.label: E
options.text: Is a gland that secretes a watery product rich in enzymes

notes.A: Not a gland description.
notes.B: It has ducts.
notes.C: Unbranched ducts make it simple and exocrine; dark (serous) and pale (mucous) units make it mixed.
notes.D: Secretory units with ducts mean it secretes a product.
notes.E: Mixed, not purely serous.

questions.why: An unbranched duct makes it a simple exocrine gland, and having dark serous units with pale mucous units makes it mixed, not purely serous.

questions.stem: You are given a specimen that is surrounded by connective tissue. Fibrous extensions from the connective tissue divides the specimen into compartments. The specimen has several clusters of epithelial cells embedded completely in a connective tissue stroma. The cell clusters are dark-stained with round nuclei that were either central or basally located. The specimen has epithelially lined passages with several branches that link the cell clusters to an epithelial-lined surface. The specimen

options.label: A
options.text: Is a simple endocrine gland with serous secretory units

options.label: B
options.text: Is a compound exocrine gland with serous secretory units

options.label: C
options.text: Is likely to be a discrete gland/a major salivary gland

options.label: D
options.text: Is a compound gland that secretes a watery product rich in enzymes

notes.A: Endocrine products enter interstitial fluid and blood without ducts. The branched passages here indicate compound exocrine secretion.
notes.B: A branched duct system defines the compound arrangement, and the dark units with round nuclei suggest serous cells.
notes.C: The lobulated, compound serous architecture is consistent with a discrete major salivary gland, particularly the parotid.
notes.D: Serous cells usually release a watery, protein-rich secretion. In the parotid this includes digestive enzymes such as amylase.

questions.why: Branched ducts reaching an epithelial surface identify a compound exocrine gland. Dark secretory cells with round nuclei fit a serous gland, such as the parotid.

questions.stem: Merocrine secretion:

options.label: A
options.text: Is synonymous with eccrine secretion

options.label: B
options.text: Involves exocytosis via the apical membrane of cells

options.label: C
options.text: Involves secretion of part of the apical cytoplasm of cells

options.label: D
options.text: Involves secretion of whole cells and their contents

options.label: E
options.text: Is the most commonly found sort of exocrine secretion

notes.A: Some histology texts use eccrine for the exocytotic mode. The term also names the sweat glands that use this mechanism.
notes.B: A secretory vesicle fuses with the apical membrane and releases its contents without loss of the cell apex.
notes.C: Release of membrane-bound apical cytoplasm describes apocrine secretion, as in mammary lipid release.
notes.D: Holocrine secretion involves disintegration of whole cells, as in the sebaceous glands.
notes.E: Merocrine secretion is the commonest exocrine release mechanism and is used by salivary and pancreatic acinar cells.

questions.why: Merocrine secretion releases a vesicle’s contents by exocytosis while the cell remains intact. It is common in exocrine glands such as the salivary glands.

questions.stem: Specimens A and B are made up of secretory epithelial cells, ducts and connective tissue. Both specimens have a combination of tubular and round secretory units. The secretory units are dark- stained with round nuclei that were either central or basally located. A and B have ducts with several branches that lead into other structures. Specimens A and B are surrounded by connective tissue. Fibrous extensions from the connective tissue divides the specimen into compartments. In addition specimen B has small clusters of cells of secretory cells that lack ducts and are closely associated with blood vessels

options.label: A
options.text: Specimens A and B are both exocrine with serous secretory units

options.label: B
options.text: Specimens A is solely serous-secreting whereas B is both exocrine and endocrine

options.label: C
options.text: Specimens A and B are the parotid and pancreas respectively

options.label: D
options.text: Specimens A and B are the pancreas and parotid respectively

options.label: E
options.text: Specimens A and B are compound tubuloalveolar merocrine glands

notes.A: Both specimens have an exocrine component with serous cells organised around small lumina connected to ducts.
notes.B: Parotid tissue is serous and exocrine. Pancreas has exocrine acini and separate endocrine islets.
notes.C: The islet-like clusters identify the second specimen as pancreas. The first fits the purely exocrine parotid.
notes.D: This reverses the identification. Islets are present in the pancreas, while parotid tissue lacks an endocrine component.
notes.E: The described exocrine components have branching ducts and tubuloacinar units that secrete by exocytosis.

questions.why: Branched ducts and serous secretory units fit both parotid and exocrine pancreas. Ductless cell clusters closely associated with capillaries identify the endocrine islets of the pancreas.

questions.stem: Ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium with goblet cells is found in the:

options.label: A
options.text: Nasal cavity and larynx and secondary bronchi

options.label: B
options.text: Trachea, membranous urethra, vas deferens

options.label: C
options.text: Primary bronchi, terminal bronchioles and the epiglottis

options.label: D
options.text: Membranous urethra, epididymis, Trachea

options.label: E
options.text: Penile urethra, primary bronchi and respiratory bronchioles

notes.A: This respiratory lining occurs in most of the nasal cavity, parts of the larynx and the secondary bronchi.
notes.B: The trachea has respiratory epithelium. The membranous urethra and vas deferens have different columnar linings.
notes.C: Primary bronchi have respiratory epithelium. Terminal bronchioles usually have a simple cuboidal or low columnar lining with club cells.
notes.D: The trachea fits, but the epididymis has stereocilia and the membranous urethra lacks the typical goblet-cell respiratory lining.
notes.E: Primary bronchi fit. The penile urethra has a different columnar lining, and respiratory bronchioles have cuboidal and alveolar regions.

questions.why: Ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium with goblet cells lines much of the conducting airway. It helps humidify inspired air and moves mucus containing trapped particles toward the pharynx.

questions.stem: A basal lamina:

options.label: A
options.text: Is a cellular layer secreted by epithelial tissues only

options.label: B
options.text: Separates epithelium from underlying connective tissue

options.label: C
options.text: Is believed to be secreted by the muscle and nerve cells

options.label: D
options.text: Contains non-fibrous collagen

options.label: E
options.text: Contains PAS positive glycoproteins

notes.A: It is acellular, and muscle and nerve cells also make one.
notes.B: It separates epithelium from the underlying connective tissue.
notes.C: Muscle and Schwann cells secrete an external lamina of the same kind.
notes.D: Its collagen is non-fibrillar type IV.
notes.E: Its glycoproteins stain with PAS.

questions.why: The basal lamina is an acellular layer of type IV collagen, laminin and PAS-positive glycoproteins under epithelium; muscle, nerve (Schwann) and fat cells make a similar external lamina.

questions.stem: Specializations of the surfaces of epithelial cells that permit passage of small molecular weight particles through cell membranes of contiguous cells are:

options.label: A
options.text: Gap junctions

options.label: B
options.text: Tight junctions

options.label: C
options.text: Desmosomes

options.label: D
options.text: Junctional complexes

options.label: E
options.text: Not known to exist in human tissue

questions.why: Gap junctions are paired connexon channels that link neighbouring cytoplasms. They allow ions and small molecules to move between cells and can coordinate electrical or metabolic activity.

notes.B: Tight junctions restrict movement through the space between cells. They do not provide a channel between their cytoplasms.
notes.C: Desmosomes connect intermediate filaments for mechanical strength. They have no channel for intercellular passage of solutes.
notes.D: The classical junctional complex includes tight and adherens junctions and desmosomes. Gap junctions are the specific intercellular channels.
notes.E: Human tissues contain gap junctions, for example in cardiac muscle where they help propagate electrical activity between cells.

questions.stem: The oesophagus:

options.label: A
options.text: Contains glands in the lamina propria and only smooth muscle in the terminal portion

options.label: B
options.text: The muscularis in the lower 1/3 is made up of smooth muscle and skeletal muscle

options.label: C
options.text: The muscularis in the upper 1/3 is made up of only skeletal muscle

notes.A: Mucous glands can occur in the lamina propria near the ends, and the terminal muscularis externa is smooth muscle.
notes.B: The middle portion typically has a mixture of skeletal and smooth muscle. The inferior portion is predominantly smooth muscle.
notes.C: The proximal muscularis externa is skeletal muscle, with a transition to mixed muscle farther down.

questions.why: Oesophageal muscularis externa changes from skeletal muscle proximally through a mixed middle segment to smooth muscle distally. Mucous cardiac glands may occur in the lamina propria near the ends.

questions.stem: The ureter:

options.label: A
options.text: Is lined partly by Transitional epithelium and pseudostratified columnar epithelium

options.label: B
options.text: Has long mucosal folds, giving its lumen a stellate appearance in cross sections

options.label: C
options.text: Has neither a muscularis mucosae nor a submucosa in their walls

options.label: D
options.text: Has a muscular arrangement that is similar to the muscularis of the gastrointestinal tract

options.label: E
options.text: Has dense collagenous connective tissue with glands

notes.A: Transitional only.
notes.B: Longitudinal mucosal folds give a star-shaped lumen when empty.
notes.C: It lacks both a muscularis mucosae and a distinct submucosa.
notes.D: Its upper part is inner longitudinal, outer circular, the reverse of the gut.
notes.E: Its adventitia is fibroelastic and has no glands.

questions.why: The ureter has transitional epithelium in stellate folds, no muscularis mucosae or submucosa, and an inner longitudinal and outer circular muscle coat, the reverse of the gut.

questions.stem: A purely serous gland possessing no striated ducts, but having long intercalated ducts and centrocinar cells, is

options.label: A
options.text: The submandibular

options.label: B
options.text: The pancreas

options.label: C
options.text: The sublingual

options.label: D
options.text: The parotid

options.label: E
options.text: Brunner’s

questions.why: Centroacinar cells are the beginning of pancreatic intercalated ducts within serous acini. The exocrine pancreas has no striated ducts, which helps distinguish it from parotid tissue.

notes.A: Submandibular glands are mixed, predominantly serous, and have prominent striated ducts for modifying saliva.
notes.C: Sublingual glands have predominantly mucous secretory units. They lack the pancreatic pattern of ducts starting inside acini.
notes.D: The parotid is predominantly serous and has intercalated ducts, but striated ducts are present and centroacinar cells are absent.
notes.E: Brunner’s glands are mucous glands in the duodenal submucosa. Their secretions help protect against gastric acid.

questions.stem: Functions of cartilage include:

options.label: A
options.text: Provision of an embryonic model prior to the development of long bones

options.label: B
options.text: Provision of rigidity to soft tissues requiring support

options.label: C
options.text: Allowing long bones to increase in length

options.label: D
options.text: Provision of a smooth surface for epiphyses of articulating joints

options.label: E
options.text: Maintenance of tubular shape of structures in the respiratory tract

notes.A: Hyaline cartilage forms an embryonic model that is progressively replaced by bone during endochondral ossification.
notes.B: Cartilage has a resilient extracellular matrix that gives shape and support to structures such as the nose.
notes.C: Growth plate chondrocytes proliferate and enlarge before their matrix is replaced by bone, extending the shaft.
notes.D: Smooth articular cartilage covers bony ends in synovial joints and helps distribute load with low friction.
notes.E: Cartilage rings or plates support the trachea and larger bronchi and help keep their airways open.

questions.why: Cartilage provides flexible support, low-friction joint surfaces and a template for endochondral bone formation. Growth plate cartilage allows many long bones to increase in length.

questions.stem: The growth spurt at puberty is due to cell proliferation and hypertrophy in the:

options.label: A
options.text: Epiphysis

options.label: B
options.text: Epiphyseal line

options.label: C
options.text: Dense bone

options.label: D
options.text: Epiphyseal plate

options.label: E
options.text: Spongy bone

notes.A: The epiphysis is the bony end region. The growth plate lies between it and the metaphysis during growth.
notes.B: The epiphyseal line is the remnant after plate closure and lacks a proliferating cartilage zone.
notes.C: Dense cortical bone can grow in thickness by apposition, while longitudinal growth depends on the cartilage plate.
notes.D: The growth plate has proliferating and hypertrophic zones whose cartilage production and replacement lengthen the bone.
notes.E: Trabecular bone remodels and accumulates below the plate. The growth-related proliferation and hypertrophy occur in cartilage.

questions.why: Longitudinal growth accelerates at puberty when growth plate chondrocytes proliferate and hypertrophy. Endochondral replacement of cartilage on the metaphyseal side progressively lengthens the bone.

questions.stem: Connective tissue fibres and glycosaminoglycans are synthesized by:

options.label: A
options.text: Macrophages and fibroblasts

options.label: B
options.text: Mast cells and reticular cells

options.label: C
options.text: Fibroblasts and reticular cells

options.label: D
options.text: Plasma cells, fibroblasts and reticular cells

options.label: E
options.text: Only fibroblasts

notes.A: Fibroblasts make extracellular matrix. Macrophages primarily engulf material and produce signals that can regulate matrix turnover.
notes.B: Reticular cells produce stroma. Mast cells contain granules rich in substances such as histamine and heparin and are not principal matrix builders.
notes.C: Fibroblasts produce matrix broadly, and specialised reticular cells build the type III collagen networks of certain stromal tissues.
notes.D: Plasma cells secrete immunoglobulins, whereas fibroblasts and reticular stromal cells are the relevant matrix-producing populations here.
notes.E: Reticular cells also make supporting matrix in certain organs, even though they are specialised members of the fibroblast lineage.

questions.why: Fibroblasts synthesise the fibres and glycosaminoglycan-rich ground substance of connective tissue. Reticular stromal cells are specialised fibroblast-like cells that produce supporting reticular fibres in certain organs.

questions.stem: Elastic connective tissue:

options.label: A
options.text: Is present in adults and foetuses

options.label: B
options.text: Is present only in foetuses

options.label: C
options.text: Is typical of the umbilical cord and placenta

options.label: D
options.text: Contains stellate fibroblasts and a mucoid ground substance

options.label: E
options.text: Contains jelly-like intercellular substance with collagenous fibers

notes.A: Elastic fibres form during development and persist in adult tissues where stretch and recoil are needed.
notes.B: Adults retain elastin-rich structures, for example the ligamenta flava and elastic lamellae of large arteries.
notes.C: The umbilical cord is characterised by Wharton’s jelly, a mucous connective tissue rich in hydrated ground substance.
notes.D: Stellate cells in mucoid ground substance describe mucous connective tissue, especially in the umbilical cord.
notes.E: A jelly-like ground substance with collagen fibres is typical of mucous connective tissue. Elastic tissue has prominent elastic fibres.

questions.why: Elastic connective tissue contains abundant elastic fibres that permit stretching and recoil. Elastic fibres develop before birth and remain important in structures such as the adult ligamenta flava.

questions.stem: Articular cartilages:

options.label: A
options.text: Are located between the ribs and are nourished by their blood vessels

options.label: B
options.text: Are located at the point where the sternum makes contact with the clavicle

options.label: C
options.text: Are located at the ends of long bones and are nourished by synovial fluid

options.label: D
options.text: Are located between the epiphysis and diaphysis

options.label: E
options.text: Contain a lot of elastic fibres and are found in the septum of the nose

notes.A: Costal cartilage.
notes.B: The sternoclavicular joint has fibrocartilage.
notes.C: Articular cartilage covers the bone ends and is nourished by synovial fluid.
notes.D: The epiphyseal plate.
notes.E: Elastic cartilage; the septum is hyaline.

questions.why: Articular cartilage is avascular hyaline cartilage on the ends of long bones, nourished by diffusion from synovial fluid.

questions.stem: Features of an osteon:

options.label: A
options.text: A central canal containing blood vessels, nerves and osteocytes

options.label: B
options.text: Concentric lamellae of matrix and osteocytes in lacunae

options.label: C
options.text: A central canal containing blood vessels and bony lamellae

options.label: D
options.text: A central canal containing osteocytes, canaliculi and nerves

notes.A: The canal contains vessels, nerves and connective tissue. Osteocytes are embedded in lacunae in the surrounding mineralised matrix.
notes.B: Concentric lamellae form the osteon around its central canal, and osteocytes occupy lacunae between lamellae.
notes.C: Vessels lie within the canal, while bony lamellae form the surrounding cylindrical wall of the osteon.
notes.D: Canaliculi run through bone matrix between lacunae. The canal itself carries vessels and nerves.

questions.why: An osteon in compact bone has concentric lamellae around a central neurovascular canal. Osteocytes occupy lacunae between lamellae and communicate through processes running in canaliculi.

questions.stem: Appositional growth of cartilage:

options.label: A
options.text: Causes clones of chondrocytes to form within the core of the cartilage

options.label: B
options.text: Adds matrix to cartilage, but not cells

options.label: C
options.text: Occurs from the chondrogenic layer of the perichondrium as well as the interstitial chondrocytes

options.label: D
options.text: Is the differentiation of chondrocytes from mesenchyme

notes.A: Clones arising inside the matrix are isogenous groups produced by interstitial growth of existing chondrocytes.
notes.B: New chondroblasts are added at the surface as well as the matrix that those cells secrete.
notes.C: The chondrogenic perichondrial layer provides cells for apposition. Division of internal chondrocytes causes interstitial growth.
notes.D: Differentiation in mesenchyme describes initial cartilage formation generally. Apposition specifically adds cartilage through perichondrial progenitors at an existing surface.

questions.why: Appositional cartilage growth adds tissue at the surface. Progenitors in the inner perichondrium become chondroblasts and secrete matrix, whereas division of embedded chondrocytes expands cartilage internally.

questions.stem: Features of the perichondrium:

options.label: A
options.text: Presence of two layers, outer cortical and inner medullary layers

options.label: B
options.text: Responsible for appositional and interstial growth

options.label: C
options.text: Is the source of nutrients and metabolites for cartilage

options.label: D
options.text: Is a source of chondroblasts

options.label: E
options.text: Is fibrous and avascular

notes.A: The two layers are outer fibrous and inner chondrogenic. Cortex and medulla are not the names of these layers.
notes.B: The perichondrium provides cells for appositional growth. Interstitial growth comes from chondrocyte division within the matrix.
notes.C: Blood vessels in the perichondrium supply nutrients that diffuse into the avascular cartilage matrix.
notes.D: Progenitor cells in the inner layer differentiate into chondroblasts, which secrete new surface matrix.
notes.E: The outer perichondrial layer is fibrous and vascular. The underlying cartilage is the avascular tissue.

questions.why: The perichondrium has an outer fibrous layer and an inner chondrogenic layer. Its vessels supply nutrients by diffusion, and its inner progenitors add cartilage at the surface.

questions.stem: You suspect a cartilage sample is from the symphysis pubis because:

options.label: A
options.text: It contains alternating layers of collagen fibers and chondrocytes

options.label: B
options.text: It contains Hyaline cartilage with chondrocytes that occur singly

options.label: C
options.text: It contains fibrocartilage

options.label: D
options.text: It contains elastic cartilage

options.label: E
options.text: It has numerous chondroblasts and few collagen fibers

notes.A: Rows of chondrocytes between thick collagen bundles are characteristic of the fibrocartilaginous disc.
notes.B: Thin hyaline cartilage covers the pubic articular surfaces, but the disc itself has collagen-rich fibrocartilage.
notes.C: Fibrocartilage forms the central pad connecting the pubic bones in this secondary cartilaginous joint.
notes.D: Elastic cartilage contains a prominent elastic fibre network and is characteristic of sites such as the auricle.
notes.E: The mature symphyseal disc has abundant coarse collagen bundles and established chondrocytes in lacunae.

questions.why: The intervening disc of the pubic symphysis is fibrocartilage. Its thick collagen bundles and rows of chondrocytes help the joint resist tension and compression.

questions.stem: Collagen type III is abundant in the:

options.label: A
options.text: Spleen and lymph nodes

options.label: B
options.text: Lymph nodes and thymus

options.label: C
options.text: Red bone marrow and kidney

options.label: D
options.text: Liver and lung

options.label: E
options.text: Kidney and haematopoietic tissues

notes.A: The spleen and lymph nodes have reticular fibre networks that support the cells of their parenchyma.
notes.B: Lymph nodes have reticular stroma, but the thymic parenchyma uses an epithelial reticular framework as its main support.
notes.C: Reticular fibres support blood-forming marrow and are found among the stromal fibres of the kidney.
notes.D: Reticular fibres support hepatic plates and form part of delicate connective tissue networks in the lung.
notes.E: Kidney stroma and haematopoietic tissue both have reticular fibres made chiefly from type III collagen.

questions.why: Type III collagen forms reticular fibres that support many soft organs. It is abundant in marrow, lymph nodes, spleen and delicate stromal networks of liver, lung and kidney.

questions.stem: Features of macrophages:

options.label: A
options.text: They may be fixed and non-mobile

options.label: B
options.text: They may use ameboid movement to wander through tissues

options.label: C
options.text: They are phagocytic and may be found in the lungs

options.label: D
options.text: They possess large lysosomes and are present in the liver

options.label: E
options.text: They can be identified by their active engulfment of injected dyes

notes.A: Some tissue macrophages remain relatively fixed in their local environment, such as Kupffer cells associated with liver sinusoids.
notes.B: Migratory macrophages can move through tissues by amoeboid movement in response to inflammatory signals.
notes.C: Alveolar macrophages phagocytose inhaled particles and microbes on the air-facing surfaces of the lung.
notes.D: Lysosomes help degrade ingested material. Kupffer cells are macrophages associated with hepatic sinusoids.
notes.E: Phagocytic uptake of appropriate vital dyes or particulate tracers can reveal macrophages in classical histology demonstrations.

questions.why: Macrophages are tissue phagocytes with abundant lysosomes. Some remain resident at specialised sites, while others migrate through connective tissue to clear microbes and cellular debris.

questions.stem: Interstitial growth of cartilage involves:

options.label: A
options.text: Mitosis and production of extracellular matrix

options.label: B
options.text: Growth of cells from the perichondrium

options.label: C
options.text: Growth of daughter cells deep in the matrix

options.label: D
options.text: Formation of isogenous cells

options.label: E
options.text: Formation of territorial matrix

notes.A: Mitosis provides new chondrocytes, and their matrix secretion increases the volume of cartilage from within.
notes.B: Perichondrial progenitors add cartilage at its surface, a mechanism known as appositional growth.
notes.C: Existing chondrocytes can divide within lacunae, leaving neighbouring daughter cells surrounded by cartilage matrix.
notes.D: An isogenous group forms from division of a single chondrocyte, so its clustered cells share a lineage.
notes.E: New matrix laid down close to lacunae contributes to the territorial matrix surrounding chondrocytes or cell groups.

questions.why: In interstitial growth, chondrocytes divide within existing cartilage matrix and form isogenous groups. Their secretion of additional matrix separates the daughter cells and expands the tissue internally.

questions.stem: Aponeuroses of the anterior abdominal wall:

options.label: A
options.text: Are regular dense connective tissue

options.label: B
options.text: Are irregular dense connective tissue

options.label: C
options.text: Are loose connective tissue

options.label: D
options.text: Resemble tendons in structure

options.label: E
options.text: Are found at the origin or insertion of skeletal muscles

notes.A: Their collagen fibres are arranged in organised layers adapted to carry tension from the abdominal muscles.
notes.B: Dense irregular tissue has less consistently aligned bundles, whereas aponeurotic layers have fibres oriented along lines of muscle pull.
notes.C: Loose connective tissue contains sparser fibres and more ground substance. An aponeurosis is a dense load-transmitting sheet.
notes.D: Like cord-like tendons, aponeuroses use dense regular collagen to transmit force, but their attachments are broad and flat.
notes.E: A skeletal muscle can take origin from or insert into an aponeurosis, which passes its force to another structure.

questions.why: Abdominal aponeuroses are broad, flat tendons of dense collagenous connective tissue. Their organised fibres transmit muscle tension across the abdominal wall and contribute to structures such as the linea alba.

questions.stem: About adipose tissue:

options.label: A
options.text: Is made up of fibers only and constitutes up to 40% or more of the total body weight in infants

options.label: B
options.text: Constitutes up to 20% or more of the total body weight in adults and is highly cellular

options.label: C
options.text: Provides thermal insulation, serves as metabolic fuel and is highly phagocytic

options.label: D
options.text: Is an important reservoir of energy

options.label: E
options.text: Acts as shock absorbers in the soles of the feet

notes.A: Adipose tissue is highly cellular. Its principal elements are adipocytes supported by a fine connective tissue framework.
notes.B: Adipocytes dominate the tissue. Body fat can make up about one-fifth or more of adult weight, with substantial individual variation.
notes.C: Insulation and stored metabolic fuel are normal roles. Phagocytosis is characteristic of macrophages rather than adipocytes.
notes.D: Adipocytes store triglycerides and can release fatty acids for use as fuel when energy demand rises.
notes.E: Fat pads in the soles cushion bony structures and help distribute mechanical loads during walking and standing.

questions.why: White adipose tissue is made chiefly of lipid-storing adipocytes. It serves as an energy reserve, limits heat loss and cushions sites exposed to pressure, including the soles.

questions.stem: Brown fat cells:

options.label: A
options.text: Contain single large lipid droplet and are mainly found in adults

options.label: B
options.text: Contain many small lipid droplets and are mainly found in foetuses

options.label: C
options.text: Are more numerous than white fat cells

options.label: D
options.text: Are not under nervous regulation and depend solely on hormonal activity

options.label: E
options.text: Form an insulating layer deep to the dermis of the skin

notes.A: One large lipid droplet characterises a white adipocyte. Brown adipocytes have several droplets and many mitochondria.
notes.B: Developing fetuses and newborns have conspicuous multilocular brown adipose deposits that support heat production after birth.
notes.C: White adipose tissue is much more abundant overall. Brown adipocytes are concentrated in smaller specialised depots.
notes.D: Sympathetic noradrenergic input activates brown adipose thermogenesis, especially during cold exposure.
notes.E: Subcutaneous insulation is mainly provided by white fat. Brown fat specialises in generating heat through uncoupled respiration.

questions.why: Brown adipocytes have many small lipid droplets and abundant mitochondria for thermogenesis. Brown fat is prominent in late fetal and newborn life and persists in variable amounts in adults.

questions.stem: Scar tissue is a type of:

options.label: A
options.text: Epithelium and connective tissue

options.label: B
options.text: Connective tissue

options.label: C
options.text: Muscle only

options.label: D
options.text: Nervous tissue

options.label: E
options.text: Epithelium, connective tissue and muscular tissue in varying proportions

notes.A: Epithelium can cover a healed surface, but the collagen-rich scar beneath it is connective tissue.
notes.B: Fibroblasts lay down extracellular collagen, which remodels into the dense connective tissue of a mature scar.
notes.C: Fibrosis can replace damaged muscle, but the scar consists primarily of collagen-rich connective tissue.
notes.D: Nervous tissue contains neurons and supporting cells. A typical fibrous scar is chiefly fibroblast-produced extracellular matrix.
notes.E: Different tissues can border or cover a scar. The scar proper is the collagenous connective tissue formed during repair.

questions.why: A mature scar is collagen-rich connective tissue deposited by fibroblasts during repair. It replaces tissue that did not regenerate and can restore mechanical continuity.

questions.stem: In endochondral ossification at the primary centre, the stated order is correct:

options.label: A
options.text: First -A collar of bone is laid down around the hyaline cartilage model just deep to the periosteum

options.label: B
options.text: Second- Periosteal bud invades the center of the diaphysis

options.label: C
options.text: Third- Cartilage in the diaphysis calcifies and contains cavities

options.label: D
options.text: Fourth- Perichondrium becomes more vascularized and becomes a periosteum

options.label: E
options.text: Fifth- Osteoclasts remove the bone from the center of the diaphysis, leaving a medullary cavity which then houses marrow

notes.B: It comes third.
notes.C: It comes second.
notes.D: It happens at the start.

questions.why: Order: bone collar forms as perichondrium becomes periosteum; central cartilage calcifies; periosteal bud invades; osteoclasts hollow the marrow cavity.

questions.stem: The shape of the external ear is maintained by:

options.label: A
options.text: Areolar tissue

options.label: B
options.text: Fibrocartilage

options.label: C
options.text: Skeletal muscle

options.label: D
options.text: Articular cartilage

options.label: E
options.text: Elastic cartilage

questions.why: Elastic cartilage provides the resilient framework of the auricle. Its elastin-rich matrix bends under pressure and then recoils to maintain the outer ear’s shape.

notes.A: Areolar connective tissue supports skin and small structures but is too yielding to form the auricle’s main framework.
notes.B: Fibrocartilage contains coarse collagen bundles adapted for load bearing, as in intervertebral discs and the pubic symphysis.
notes.C: Small auricular muscles may move the ear, but the shape of the pinna is maintained by cartilage.
notes.D: Articular cartilage covers bony ends in joints. The auricle requires a flexible framework enriched in elastic fibres.

questions.stem: A male Anatomy Professor examined a specimen from an unknown location. He concluded that the specimen contained 2 types of fibres A and B. A had peripherally located flattened nuclei, cross striations and cylindrical-shaped multinucleated fibres with rounded ends; fibre B had centrally located nuclei, spindle-shaped mononucleated fibres, absence of cross striations and intercalated disks: A and B were

options.label: A
options.text: Skeletal muscle and smooth muscle respectively

options.label: B
options.text: Smooth muscle and smooth muscle respectively

options.label: C
options.text: Skeletal muscle and collagen type I respectively

options.label: D
options.text: Cardiac muscle and collagen type I respectively

options.label: E
options.text: Cardiac muscle and smooth muscle respectively

notes.A: The first fibre has peripheral nuclei and cross-striations, while the second shows the central nucleus and taper of smooth muscle.
notes.B: Smooth muscle cells have a central nucleus and lack cross-striations. Those features do not match the first fibre.
notes.C: Collagen is extracellular and has no nucleus. The second structure is a nucleated spindle-shaped cell.
notes.D: Cardiac myocytes usually have central nuclei and intercalated discs. Collagen cannot account for the central nucleus of the second fibre.
notes.E: The second fibre fits smooth muscle, but peripheral nuclei and multinucleation of the first fibre favour skeletal muscle.

questions.why: Long striated fibres with peripheral nuclei identify skeletal muscle. Spindle-shaped cells with one central nucleus and no cross-striations or intercalated discs identify smooth muscle.

questions.stem: Cardiac muscle fibres:

options.label: A
options.text: Voluntary, spindle-shaped and striated

options.label: B
options.text: Parallel to each other with peripherally-located nuclei

options.label: C
options.text: Composed of chains of cells each with a single nucleus

options.label: D
options.text: Not striated but has intercalated disks

notes.A: Involuntary, branched.
notes.B: Branched, central nuclei.
notes.C: Each cell in the chain has a single (sometimes two) central nucleus.
notes.D: Striated.

questions.why: Cardiac muscle is involuntary and striated: branched chains of cells, each with one or two central nuclei, joined end to end by intercalated discs.

questions.stem: About muscle tissue:

options.label: A
options.text: Smooth muscle cells are connected by gap junctions and desmosomes

options.label: B
options.text: Cardiac muscle has peripherally situated nuclei

options.label: C
options.text: Smooth muscle cells are connected by tight junctions

options.label: D
options.text: Skeletal muscle may be associated with the viscera

options.label: E
options.text: Smooth muscle is found in the blood vessels

notes.A: Gap junctions electrically couple many smooth muscle cells. Mechanical cell contacts can include desmosome-like junctions in some smooth muscles.
notes.B: Cardiomyocyte nuclei are usually central. Peripheral nuclei are characteristic of mature skeletal muscle fibres.
notes.C: Smooth muscle uses gap junctions for communication. Sealing tight junctions are more characteristic of epithelial barriers.
notes.D: Some visceral structures contain skeletal muscle. Examples include the upper oesophagus and parts of the pharynx.
notes.E: Smooth muscle in the tunica media of many vessels adjusts lumen diameter and contributes to vascular tone.

questions.why: Smooth muscle is found in blood vessels and many viscera, and gap junctions can coordinate neighbouring cells. Skeletal muscle also occurs in some visceral structures, including the upper oesophagus.

questions.stem: Skeletal muscle fibres:

options.label: A
options.text: Voluntary, binucleated and striated

options.label: B
options.text: Parallel to each other

options.label: C
options.text: Composed of spindle-shaped cells that branch and rejoin

options.label: D
options.text: Not striated but has intercalated disks

options.label: E
options.text: Present in the diaphragm, soft palate, tongue and ureter

notes.A: Skeletal fibres are usually striated and under voluntary control, but a mature fibre normally has many nuclei.
notes.B: Fibres generally lie parallel within a fascicle, so their tension acts along a shared direction.
notes.C: Branching and rejoining are characteristic of cardiac muscle. Skeletal fibres are typically long, cylindrical and unbranched.
notes.D: Skeletal fibres have cross-striations and lack intercalated discs. Cardiac muscle has both striations and intercalated discs.
notes.E: The diaphragm, soft palate and tongue contain skeletal muscle. The ureter propels urine with smooth muscle.

questions.why: Skeletal muscle fibres are long, parallel, striated cells formed by fusion of myoblasts. Mature fibres usually contain many nuclei arranged near the edge of the cell.

questions.stem: About nervous tissue:

options.label: A
options.text: Neurons are characterized by irritability

options.label: B
options.text: Neurons have processes

options.label: C
options.text: Dendrites are usually more numerous than axons

options.label: D
options.text: Axons are transmitters of impulses away from the perikarya

options.label: E
options.text: Axons are processes of nerve cells

notes.A: Neuronal excitability is the ability to alter membrane potential in response to stimuli and, when appropriate, generate an action potential.
notes.B: Neurons have cellular extensions called processes. These include dendrites and axons with different signalling roles.
notes.C: Most multipolar neurons have many dendrites and a single axon, although neuronal shapes differ between populations.
notes.D: Axons usually conduct action potentials away from the cell body toward synapses or other target structures.
notes.E: An axon is a neuronal process specialised for carrying signals over a distance from the cell body.

questions.why: Neurons respond to stimulation and transmit signals through their specialised processes. Most have several receptive dendrites and one axon that conducts action potentials toward target cells.
